title: 1 Samuel

stories.title: 👶 1 Samuel 1
summaryBullets: Now there was a man named Elkanah who was from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim. He was the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite. (1:1).
He had two wives, one named Hannah and the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none. (1:2).
Year after year Elkanah would go up from his city to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of Hosts at Shiloh, where Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests to the LORD. (1:3).
And whenever the day came for Elkanah to present his sacrifice, he would give portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters. (1:4).
But to Hannah he would give a double portion, for he loved her even though the LORD had closed her womb. (1:5).
Because the LORD had closed Hannah’s womb, her rival would provoke her viciously to taunt her. (1:6).
And this went on year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the house of the LORD, her rival taunted her until she wept and would not eat. (1:7).
“Hannah, why are you crying?” her husband Elkanah asked. “Why won’t you eat? Why is your heart so grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (1:8).
So after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh, Hannah stood up. Now Eli the priest was sitting on a chair by the doorpost of the temple of the LORD. (1:9).
In her bitter distress, Hannah prayed to the LORD and wept with many tears. (1:10).

And she made a vow, saying, “O LORD of Hosts, if only You will look upon the affliction of Your maidservant and remember me, not forgetting Your maidservant but giving her a son, then I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall ever touch his head.” (1:11).
As Hannah kept on praying before the LORD, Eli watched her mouth. (1:12).
Hannah was praying in her heart, and though her lips were moving, her voice could not be heard. So Eli thought she was drunk (1:13).
and said to her, “How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine!” (1:14).
“No, my lord,” Hannah replied. “I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have not had any wine or strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the LORD. (1:15).
Do not take your servant for a wicked woman, for all this time I have been praying out of the depth of my anguish and grief.” (1:16).
“Go in peace,” Eli replied, “and may the God of Israel grant the petition you have asked of Him.” (1:17).
“May your maidservant find favor with you,” said Hannah. Then she went on her way, and she began to eat, and her face was no longer downcast. (1:18).
The next morning they got up early to bow in worship before the LORD, and then they returned home to Ramah. And Elkanah had relations with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her. (1:19).
So in the course of time, Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel,saying, “Because I have asked for him from the LORD.” (1:20).
Then Elkanah and all his house went up to make the annual sacrifice to the LORD and to fulfill his vow, (1:21).
but Hannah did not go. “After the boy is weaned,” she said to her husband, “I will take him to appear before the LORD and to stay there permanently.” (1:22).

“Do what you think is best,” her husband Elkanah replied, “and stay here until you have weaned him. Only may the LORD confirm His word.” So Hannah stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him. (1:23).

Once she had weaned him, Hannah took the boy with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine. Though the boy was still young, she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. (1:24).
And when they had slaughtered the bull, they brought the boy to Eli. (1:25).
“Please, my lord,” said Hannah, “as surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD. (1:26).
I prayed for this boy, and since the LORD has granted me what I asked of Him, (1:27).
I now dedicate the boy to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is dedicated to the LORD.” So they worshiped the LORD there. (1:28).
crossRefs: Genesis 30:1-2,22-24: Rachel's barrenness and her cry for children, until God remembers her and opens her womb.
Judges 13:2-7: Manoah's barren wife is told she will bear a son who is to be a Nazirite from the womb.
Numbers 6:1-8: The law of the Nazirite vow: no wine, no razor on the head, no contact with a dead body.
Numbers 30:3-15: The rules governing a woman's vow, and when a husband may confirm it or annul it.
Joshua 18:1: The whole assembly gathers at Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting there.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נָזִיר (nazir), from נָזַר (nazar), to separate
translationNotes.note: Hannah's vow in verse 11 gives the boy to the LORD for life and adds that no razor shall touch his head. Numbers 6:1-21 sets out the full vow: nothing at all from the grapevine, not wine, not vinegar, not grapes fresh or dried, not even skins or seeds; no razor for the whole term; and no going near a dead body, not even a father's or mother's. It was normally taken for a fixed period and closed at the sanctuary with offerings and the shaving of the head. Hannah imposes it for life on a child not yet conceived, which is what Samson's parents were told in Judges 13:5.

Verses 3 and 11 carry the first appearance of this title anywhere in Scripture. Tsava means an army or a fighting force, and its plural is the word behind Hosts, so the title names God as commander of armies: Israel's fighting men in one place (17:45) and the armies of heaven in another (1 Kings 22:19). It becomes the standard title in the prophets, used more than two hundred times in Isaiah, Jeremiah and Zechariah alone. It enters the book at Shiloh, at a sanctuary that is about to lose a war.

Verse 6 uses a word that means rival or adversary for Peninnah, the other wife. A childless woman had no standing and no security in old age, and a household with two wives put the two women in direct competition, which is what Sarah and Hagar, and Leah and Rachel, both show. The law assumes such households exist and limits the damage: Deuteronomy 21:15-17 forbids a man with a loved wife and an unloved one to pass over the unloved wife's firstborn when he divides his property. Verse 5 has Elkanah give Hannah a double portion at the feast, in public, which is exactly the sort of thing verse 6 says Peninnah made her pay for.

Verses 22 to 24 turn on a date most readers pass over. Children in that world were nursed for two to three years, and weaning was a milestone marked with a feast; Genesis 21:8 has Abraham hold one on the day Isaac was weaned. So Samuel is a small child, not an infant and not a youth, when Hannah walks him up to Shiloh with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour and a skin of wine, and leaves him there.
The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).

stories.keyTakeaway: Elkanah's wife Hannah, unable to have children, prays desperately at Shiloh and vows to give her son to the Lord if granted one; the Lord remembers her, she bears Samuel, and after weaning him she brings him to Eli to serve at the house of the Lord.

stories.title: 👶 1 Samuel 2
summaryBullets: At that time Hannah prayed: “My heart rejoices in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies, for I rejoice in Your salvation. (2:1).
There is no one holy like the LORD. Indeed, there is no one besides You! And there is no Rock like our God. (2:2).
Do not boast so proudly, or let arrogance come from your mouth, for the LORD is a God who knows, and by Him actions are weighed. (2:3).
The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble are equipped with strength. (2:4).
The well-fed hire themselves out for food, but the starving hunger no more. The barren woman gives birth to seven, but she who has many sons pines away. (2:5).
The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up. (2:6).
The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts. (2:7).

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor. For the foundations of the earth are the LORD’s, and upon them He has set the world. (2:8).
He guards the steps of His faithful ones, but the wicked perish in darkness; for by his own strength shall no man prevail. (2:9).

Those who oppose the LORD will be shattered. He will thunder from heaven against them. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.” (2:10).
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy began ministering to the LORD before Eli the priest. (2:11).
Now the sons of Eli were wicked men; they had no regard for the LORD (2:12).
or for the custom of the priests with the people. When any man offered a sacrifice, the servant of the priest would come with a three-pronged meat fork while the meat was boiling (2:13).

and plunge it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or cooking pot. And the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up. This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh. (2:14).

Even before the fat was burned, the servant of the priest would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, “Give the priest some meat to roast, because he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw.” (2:15).

And if any man said to him, “The fat must be burned first; then you may take whatever you want,” the servant would reply, “No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!” (2:16).
Thus the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD, for they were treating the LORD’s offering with contempt. (2:17).
Now Samuel was ministering before the LORD — a boy wearing a linen ephod. (2:18).
Each year his mother would make him a little robe and bring it to him when she went with her husband to offer the annual sacrifice. (2:19).
And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, saying, “May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she dedicated to the LORD.” Then they would go home. (2:20).
So the LORD attended to Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to three sons and two daughters. Meanwhile, the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD. (2:21).
Now Eli was very old, and he heard about everything his sons were doing to all Israel and how they were sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. (2:22).
“Why are you doing these things?” Eli said to his sons. “I hear about your wicked deeds from all these people. (2:23).
No, my sons; it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people. (2:24).

If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?” But they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death. (2:25).
And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man. (2:26).
Then a man of God came to Eli and told him, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Did I not clearly reveal Myself to your father’s house when they were in Egypt under Pharaoh’s house? (2:27).

And out of all the tribes of Israel I selected your father to be My priest, to offer sacrifices on My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod in My presence. I also gave to the house of your father all the food offerings of the Israelites. (2:28).

Why then do you kick at My sacrifice and offering that I have prescribed for My dwelling place? You have honored your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of all the offerings of My people Israel.’ (2:29).

Therefore, the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: ‘I did indeed say that your house and the house of your father would walk before Me forever. But now the LORD declares: Far be it from Me! For I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained. (2:30).
Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father’s house, so that no one in it will reach old age. (2:31).
You will see distress in My dwelling place. Despite all that is good in Israel, no one in your house will ever again reach old age. (2:32).
And every one of you that I do not cut off from My altar, I will cause your eyes to fail and your heart to grieve. All your descendants will die by the sword of men. (2:33).
And this sign shall come to you concerning your two sons Hophni and Phinehas: They will both die on the same day. (2:34).

Then I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind. And I will build for him an enduring house, and he will walk before My anointed one for all time. (2:35).

And everyone left in your house will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver or a morsel of bread, pleading, “Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread.”’” (2:36).
crossRefs: Luke 1:46-55: Mary's song, following Hannah's line by line in praise for the lowly lifted up and the mighty pulled down.
Leviticus 7:28-36: The breast and the right thigh of the peace offering are the priests' portion, and nothing beyond it.
Leviticus 3:16-17: All the fat belongs to the LORD, and you shall eat neither fat nor blood.
1 Kings 2:26-27: Abiathar is removed from the priesthood, fulfilling the word spoken against Eli's house at Shiloh.
Psalm 113:7-9: He raises the poor from the dust and gives the barren woman a home as the joyful mother of children.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חַטָּאת (chattat), missing the mark - עָוֹן (avon), guilt
translationNotes.note: Two different words stand behind sin in this chapter. Chattat is the failure itself, from a root meaning to miss a target; avon is the guilt that then attaches to a person and has to be dealt with. Verse 17 says the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, because they treated the offering of the LORD with contempt, and 3:13-14 uses the other word to say the guilt of Eli's house would never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering. The offence is not appetite; it is priests robbing the altar.

translationNotes.term: The priest's due and the meat fork
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַזְלֵג שְׁלֹשׁ־הַשִּׁנַּיִם (mazleg shelosh ha-shinnayim), the three-toothed fork
translationNotes.note: Verses 13 to 16 describe theft from an offering, and the reader has to know the rule being broken. Leviticus 7:31-34 gives the priest a fixed portion, the breast and the right thigh, and no more. Leviticus 3:16-17 says all the fat belongs to the LORD and must go up in smoke first, and 7:25 makes eating it a capital matter. Eli's sons send a servant with a three-pronged fork to stab into the pot and keep whatever comes up, and demand raw meat for roasting before the fat has been burned at all.

Hannah's song opens and closes on the same figure: my horn is exalted in the LORD in verse 1, and He will exalt the horn of His anointed in verse 10. The horn is an ox's or a ram's, the animal's weapon and the visible measure of its strength, so a raised horn means strength put on display and a horn cut off means power broken (Lamentations 2:3). Verse 10 is also the first place in Scripture where an anointed king is spoken of this way, in the mouth of a woman standing at Shiloh before Israel has a king at all.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֵפוֹד בָּד (efod bad), an ephod of linen
translationNotes.note: Verse 18 dresses the boy Samuel in a linen ephod. This is not the high priest's jewelled vestment of gold and coloured yarn (Exodus 28:6-14) but a plain linen version, the working dress of anyone serving before the LORD: the eighty-five priests killed at Nob wear it (22:18), and David wears one when he brings the ark up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:14). Verse 19 adds that his mother made him a little robe and brought it up to him once a year, which fixes how young he was.

The Old Testament realm of the dead; a shadowy underworld where both righteous and wicked descend (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 16:10). Not necessarily a place of torment; more a state of cessation and silence. The Septuagint and New Testament render it with the Greek word hades.

stories.keyTakeaway: Hannah praises God for lifting her from barrenness and bearing a son; meanwhile Eli's sons abuse their priestly duties while Samuel grows in favor, and a man of God tells Eli his family will lose the priesthood because they despise God's offerings.

headings.text: A Prophecy against the House of Eli

stories.title: 👶 1 Samuel 3
summaryBullets: And the boy Samuel ministered to the LORD before Eli. Now in those days the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were scarce. (3:1).
And at that time Eli, whose eyesight had grown so dim that he could not see, was lying in his room. (3:2).
Before the lamp of God had gone out, Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was located. (3:3).
Then the LORD called to Samuel, and he answered, “Here I am.” (3:4).
He ran to Eli and said, “Here I am, for you have called me.” “I did not call,” Eli replied. “Go back and lie down.” So he went and lay down. (3:5).
Once again the LORD called, “Samuel!” So Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you have called me.” “My son, I did not call,” Eli replied. “Go back and lie down.” (3:6).
Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, because the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him. (3:7).

Once again, for the third time, the LORD called to Samuel. He got up, went to Eli, and said, “Here I am, for you have called me.” Then Eli realized that it was the LORD who was calling the boy. (3:8).
“Go and lie down,” he said to Samuel, “and if He calls you, say, ‘Speak, LORD, for Your servant is listening.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place. (3:9).
Then the LORD came and stood there, calling as before, “Samuel! Samuel!” And Samuel answered, “Speak, for Your servant is listening.” (3:10).
Then the LORD said to Samuel, “I am about to do something in Israel at which the ears of all who hear it will tingle. (3:11).
On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I have spoken about his house, from beginning to end. (3:12).
I told him that I would judge his house forever for the iniquity of which he knows, because his sons blasphemed God and he did not restrain them. (3:13).
Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli, ‘The iniquity of Eli’s house shall never be atoned for by sacrifice or offering.’” (3:14).
Samuel lay down until the morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. He was afraid to tell Eli the vision, (3:15).
but Eli called to him and said, “Samuel, my son.” “Here I am,” answered Samuel. (3:16).
“What was the message He gave you?” Eli asked. “Do not hide it from me. May God punish you, and ever so severely, if you hide from me anything He said to you.” (3:17).
So Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him. “He is the LORD,” replied Eli. “Let Him do what is good in His eyes.” (3:18).
And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and He let none of Samuel’s words fall to the ground. (3:19).
So all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was confirmed as a prophet of the LORD. (3:20).
And the LORD continued to appear at Shiloh, because there He revealed Himself to Samuel by His word. (3:21).
crossRefs: Amos 8:11-12: A famine of hearing the words of the LORD, when men wander from sea to sea and do not find it.
Numbers 12:6-8: God makes Himself known to a prophet in visions and dreams, but with Moses He speaks mouth to mouth.
Jeremiah 1:4-10: The LORD calls Jeremiah while he protests that he is only a youth, and puts His words in his mouth.
1 Samuel 2:27-36: The word already spoken against Eli's house by a man of God, repeated here to the boy.
Exodus 27:20-21: Aaron and his sons keep the lamp burning before the LORD from evening to morning.

translationNotes.note: The job is defined by Exodus 7:1, where God makes Aaron Moses' navi: a mouth for someone else, who says what he is given and nothing more. Deuteronomy 18:18-22 sets the test, which is whether the thing spoken happens. Verses 19 to 21 of this chapter say the LORD let none of Samuel's words fall to the ground, and that all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew he was established as a prophet, which is the test being publicly passed.

Verse 3 is a clock, not a mood. The lamps of the golden lampstand in the holy place were tended to burn from evening until morning and were put out and cleaned at dawn (Exodus 27:20-21, Leviticus 24:2-3). Saying the lamp of God had not yet gone out places the whole scene in the last dark hour before daybreak, with the boy on duty asleep near the ark.

translationNotes.term: The doors of the house of the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הֵיכַל יְהוָה (hekhal YHWH), the temple of the LORD
translationNotes.note: Verse 3 calls Shiloh the temple of the LORD and verse 15 has Samuel open its doors in the morning, so by this time the tabernacle at Shiloh stood inside a permanent structure with doors that were shut at night. The Hebrew word hekhal covers a palace as readily as a temple and simply means a great house. Shiloh had been Israel's sanctuary since Joshua 18:1, and this chapter is the last time God speaks there.

translationNotes.term: May God do so to me and more also
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כֹּה יַעֲשֶׂה־לְּךָ אֱלֹהִים וְכֹה יוֹסִיף (koh yaaseh lekha Elohim ve-khoh yosif)
translationNotes.note: Eli's words in verse 17 are the standard Hebrew oath, and it is a self-curse with the penalty deliberately left blank: may God do such-and-such to me, and more besides, if I do otherwise. Jonathan uses it (20:13), Saul uses it (14:44), David uses it (2 Samuel 3:35), Abigail's would-be killer uses it (25:22), and Jezebel swears it against Elijah (1 Kings 19:2). Leaving the punishment unnamed was the point; naming it would have limited it.

stories.keyTakeaway: God calls Samuel three times in the night; Eli recognizes it is the Lord and instructs Samuel to listen, then the Lord tells Samuel he will judge Eli's house for failing to restrain his blasphemous sons. Samuel relays the message to Eli in the morning, and as Samuel grows up, all Israel recognizes him as a prophet of the Lord.

stories.title: 📦 1 Samuel 4
summaryBullets: Thus the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now the Israelites went out to meet the Philistines in battle and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek. (4:1).
The Philistines arrayed themselves against Israel, and as the battle spread, Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who struck down about four thousand men on the battlefield. (4:2).

When the troops returned to the camp, the elders of Israel asked, “Why has the LORD brought defeat on us before the Philistines today? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh, so that it may go with us to save us from the hand of our enemies.” (4:3).

So the people sent men to Shiloh, and they brought back the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Hosts, who sits enthroned between the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God. (4:4).
When the ark of the covenant of the LORD entered the camp, all the Israelites raised such a great shout that the ground shook. (4:5).
On hearing the noise of the shout, the Philistines asked, “What is this loud shouting in the camp of the Hebrews?” And when they realized that the ark of the LORD had entered the camp, (4:6).
the Philistines were afraid. “The gods have entered their camp!” they said. “Woe to us, for nothing like this has happened before. (4:7).
Woe to us! Who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with all kinds of plagues in the wilderness. (4:8).
Take courage and be men, O Philistines! Otherwise, you will serve the Hebrews just as they served you. Now be men and fight!” (4:9).
So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and each man fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great — thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell. (4:10).
The ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died. (4:11).
That same day a Benjamite ran from the battle line all the way to Shiloh, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. (4:12).

When he arrived, there was Eli, sitting on his chair beside the road and watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. When the man entered the city to give a report, the whole city cried out. (4:13).
Eli heard the outcry and asked, “Why this commotion?” So the man hurried over and reported to Eli. (4:14).
Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his gaze was fixed because he could not see. (4:15).
“I have just come from the battle,” the man said to Eli. “I fled from there today.” “What happened, my son?” Eli asked. (4:16).

The messenger answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are both dead, and the ark of God has been captured.” (4:17).
As soon as the ark of God was mentioned, Eli fell backward from his chair by the city gate, and being old and heavy, he broke his neck and died. And Eli had judged Israel forty years. (4:18).

Now Eli’s daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and about to give birth. When she heard the news of the capture of God’s ark and the deaths of her father-in-law and her husband, she collapsed and gave birth, for her labor pains overtook her. (4:19).
As she was dying, the women attending to her said, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son!” But she did not respond or pay any heed. (4:20).
And she named the boy Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel,” because the ark of God had been captured and her father-in-law and her husband had been killed. (4:21).
“The glory has departed from Israel,” she said, “for the ark of God has been captured.” (4:22).
crossRefs: Numbers 10:35-36: Whenever the ark set out Moses said, Arise, O LORD, and let Your enemies be scattered before You.
Deuteronomy 28:25: The LORD will cause you to be struck down before your enemies, going out one way and fleeing seven ways.
Psalm 78:56-64: God abandoned the dwelling at Shiloh, gave His strength into captivity, and His priests fell by the sword.
Jeremiah 7:12-14: Go now to My place at Shiloh and see what I did to it, and I will do the same to this house.
1 Samuel 2:34: The sign given to Eli, that Hophni and Phinehas would both die on the same day.

translationNotes.note: Verses 21 and 22 explain the name as she gives it: the glory has departed from Israel. Kavod, the word for glory, comes from a root meaning weight, so it carries the sense of substance and honour, of a person who counts for something. The dying woman does not name her son after her husband or her father-in-law, both of whom died that day; she names him after what left with the ark.

Verse 4 gives the ark its full title. The lid of the chest was a slab of gold called the kapporet, with two cherubim of hammered gold facing each other at its ends and their wings spread over it, and Exodus 25:22 and Numbers 7:89 say God met Moses and spoke from between them. Cherubim are guardian figures, not infants with wings; a pair with drawn flame is set at the gate of Eden in Genesis 3:24. Verse 3 shows Israel sending for the ark the way a man sends for a lucky charm, and the chapter records how that went.

Verses 19 to 22 report a death in labour with the exactness of someone who was there. The women attending her tell her she has a son, which was the one piece of news reckoned strong enough to rally a failing mother, and she does not answer. Rachel dies the same way and also names her son with her last breath (Genesis 35:16-18). Childbirth was the commonest cause of death for women in that world, and Scripture never treats it as anything but ordinary and terrible.

The Philistines camp at Aphek, at the head of the Yarkon springs on the coastal plain about twenty-five miles northwest of Jerusalem, where the international coast road passes through a narrow gap between the water and the hills. Whoever held it controlled the traffic. The Philistines muster there again before the battle in which Saul dies (1 Samuel 29:1), and the site was later rebuilt by Herod as Antipatris (Acts 23:31).

Israel's central sanctuary for the whole period of the judges, about twenty miles north of Jerusalem, where the tabernacle stood from Joshua 18:1 onward. This chapter is where it ends: the ark is taken and never returns there. Jeremiah 7:12-14 points back to Shiloh's ruin as the warning that a building God once named as His own can be given up.

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel is defeated by the Philistines in battle; though the ark is brought to camp and the Israelites shout, they are routed again, losing thirty thousand soldiers and the ark itself. Eli dies hearing the news, and Phinehas's widow names her newborn son Ichabod, declaring that God's glory has departed from Israel.

stories.title: 📦 1 Samuel 5
summaryBullets: After the Philistines had captured the ark of God, they took it from Ebenezer to Ashdod, (5:1).
carried it into the temple of Dagon, and set it beside his statue. (5:2).
When the people of Ashdod got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and returned him to his place. (5:3).

But when they got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD, with his head and his hands broken off and lying on the threshold. Only the torso remained. (5:4).
That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon in Ashdod do not step on the threshold. (5:5).
Now the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its vicinity, ravaging them and afflicting them with tumors. (5:6).
And when the men of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, “The ark of the God of Israel must not stay here with us, because His hand is heavy upon us and upon our god Dagon.” (5:7).

So they called together all the rulers of the Philistines and asked, “What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?” “It must be moved to Gath,” they replied. So they carried away the ark of the God of Israel. (5:8).

But after they had moved the ark to Gath, the LORD’s hand was also against that city, throwing it into great confusion and afflicting the men of the city, both young and old, with an outbreak of tumors. (5:9).
So they sent the ark of God to Ekron, but as it arrived, the Ekronites cried out, “They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!” (5:10).

Then the Ekronites called together all the rulers of the Philistines and said, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel. It must return to its place, so that it will not kill us and our people!” For a deadly confusion had pervaded the city; the hand of God was very heavy upon it. (5:11).
Those who did not die were afflicted with tumors, and the outcry of the city went up to heaven. (5:12).
crossRefs: Exodus 12:12: I will strike all the firstborn of Egypt and execute judgments on all the gods of Egypt.
Judges 16:23-30: The Philistine lords gather to sacrifice to Dagon, and Samson pulls the temple down on them.
Isaiah 46:1-2: Bel bows down and Nebo stoops; their idols are loaded on animals and carried off into captivity.
Psalm 115:4-8: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands, with mouths that do not speak and eyes that do not see.
1 Chronicles 10:10: The Philistines put Saul's armour in the house of their gods and fasten his head in the temple of Dagon.

translationNotes.term: Setting a captured god beside your own
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית דָּגוֹן (Beit Dagon), the house of Dagon
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 is a formal act, not a storage decision. Putting the emblem of a defeated nation's God in your own god's temple was how a victor published the result: their god is now a prisoner in the house of ours. Nebuchadnezzar does the same with the vessels of the temple in Jerusalem, carrying them into the treasury of his god (Daniel 1:2), and the Philistines will do it again with Saul's armour in the temple of Ashtoreth (31:10). The next three verses are the answer to it.

translationNotes.term: The hand of the LORD was heavy
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: יַד־יְהוָה (yad YHWH), the hand of the LORD
translationNotes.note: Hand is the standard Hebrew figure for power actually being applied, and it runs through this chapter and the next: verses 6, 7, 9 and 11, and again at 6:3, 5 and 9. The Philistines use it themselves in verse 7, saying His hand is harsh on us and on Dagon our god. It is the same expression used of what God did in Egypt (Exodus 9:3), which is exactly the comparison the Philistine priests reach for at 6:6.

The chief god of the Philistine cities, with temples at Ashdod, Gaza, and Beth-shan; the name is linked to dagan, grain, and his cult was tied to the harvest. Verses 3 and 4 have the image found face down before the ark twice, the second time with its head and both hands broken off on the threshold. Verse 5 records the result: from then on his priests and worshippers stepped over the threshold rather than on it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: סַרְנֵי פְלִשְׁתִּים (sarnei Pelishtim), lords of the Philistines
translationNotes.note: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron each had its own ruler, and they acted together by council rather than under one king; the title used for them, seren, is not the ordinary Hebrew word for a ruler. All five sit on or near the coastal plain southwest of Judah, on the trade road between Egypt and the north. The ark is passed from one city to the next in this chapter because no council could decide what to do with it.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Philistines place the captured ark in Dagon's temple, but the statue falls and breaks before it; God afflicts Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron with tumors and panic, forcing the rulers to decide the ark must be sent away.

stories.title: 📦 1 Samuel 6
summaryBullets: When the ark of the LORD had been in the land of the Philistines seven months, (6:1).
the Philistines summoned the priests and diviners, saying, “What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how to send it back to its place.” (6:2).

They replied, “If you return the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it away empty, but by all means return it to Him with a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and you will understand why His hand has not been lifted from you.” (6:3).

“What guilt offering should we send back to Him?” asked the Philistines. “Five gold tumors and five gold rats,” they said, “according to the number of rulers of the Philistines, since the same plague has struck both you and your rulers. (6:4).
Make images of your tumors and of the rats that are ravaging the land. Give glory to the God of Israel, and perhaps He will lift His hand from you and your gods and your land. (6:5).
Why harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened theirs? When He afflicted them, did they not send the people out so they could go on their way? (6:6).
Now, therefore, prepare one new cart with two milk cows that have never been yoked. Hitch the cows to the cart, but take their calves away and pen them up. (6:7).
Take the ark of the LORD, set it on the cart, and in a chest beside it put the gold objects you are sending back to Him as a guilt offering. Then send the ark on its way, (6:8).

but keep watching it. If it goes up the road to its homeland, toward Beth-shemesh, it is the LORD who has brought on us this great disaster. But if it does not, then we will know that it was not His hand that punished us and that it happened by chance.” (6:9).
So the men did as instructed. They took two milk cows, hitched them to the cart, and penned up their calves. (6:10).
Then they put the ark of the LORD on the cart, along with the chest containing the gold rats and the images of the tumors. (6:11).

And the cows headed straight up the road toward Beth-shemesh, staying on that one highway and lowing as they went, never straying to the right or to the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed behind them to the border of Beth-shemesh. (6:12).
Now the people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley, and when they looked up and saw the ark, they were overjoyed at the sight. (6:13).
The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there near a large rock. The people chopped up the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD. (6:14).

And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the chest containing the gold objects, and they placed them on the large rock. That day the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices to the LORD. (6:15).
And when the five rulers of the Philistines saw this, they returned to Ekron that same day. (6:16).
As a guilt offering to the LORD, the Philistines had sent back one gold tumor for each city: Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. (6:17).

The number of gold rats also corresponded to the number of Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers — the fortified cities and their outlying villages. And the large rock on which they placed the ark of the LORD stands to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh. (6:18).

But God struck down some of the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked inside the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with a great slaughter. (6:19).
The men of Beth-shemesh asked, “Who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God? To whom should the ark go up from here?” (6:20).
So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath-jearim, saying, “The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up with you.” (6:21).
crossRefs: Numbers 4:5-6,15,20: The ark is covered by Aaron before the Kohathites lift it, and they must not touch or look at the holy things, or they die.
Exodus 25:12-15: The ark's poles are set in its rings and never removed, so it is carried on the shoulder.
Exodus 8:15,32: Pharaoh sees the relief, hardens his heart, and does not listen, the pattern the Philistine priests warn against.
2 Samuel 6:6-7: Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark on a cart, and God strikes him down beside it.
Joshua 15:10: Beth-shemesh is named on Judah's northern border, the town the cows walked to.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֳפָלִים (ophalim), swellings - עַכְבָּרִים (akhbarim), mice or rats
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word covers boils, swellings or piles; the text pairs the affliction with rats overrunning the land (verses 4, 5 and 11), and 5:6 has it killing people in numbers. Swellings in the body, rats in the fields and a rising death toll are the three things a plague of this kind leaves behind, and the Philistine priests treat the two as one problem to be paid off together.

Verses 3 to 5 have the Philistine priests send back not a gift but an asham, which in Israel's law is a reparation payment for trespass against holy things: the wrong is valued in silver, restored, and a fifth added on top (Leviticus 5:14-16). What they send is five gold tumours and five gold rats, one for each city, models of the affliction offered as the price of it. Making a metal model of a diseased part and dedicating it at a shrine was ordinary practice across the ancient world.

translationNotes.term: A new cart and two milk cows
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֲגָלָה חֲדָשָׁה (agalah chadashah), a new cart
translationNotes.note: Verses 7 to 12 set up a test with the odds deliberately stacked one way. The cows have never been yoked, so they have no training to pull; they are in milk and their calves are shut up behind them, so every instinct in the animals is to turn back. The cart is new, never used for common work. If the pair walk a straight road to Beth-shemesh, lowing as they go, nothing natural explains it, and the Philistine rulers follow behind to the border to watch.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בֵּית שֶׁמֶשׁ (Beit Shemesh), house of the sun
translationNotes.note: The town lies in the Sorek valley on the border between Judah and Philistine country, in direct line of sight up the valley from Ekron, which is why the cart can be watched the whole way. It was a Levitical town (Joshua 21:16), so there were men there qualified to handle the ark, and verse 15 says the Levites took it down. Its name preserves an older Canaanite sun shrine, and centuries later King Amaziah of Judah was captured there by Israel (2 Kings 14:11-13).

The Hebrew yirah covers the whole range from plain terror to settled reverence, and this chapter uses the sharp end of it. After the deaths at Beth-shemesh the men there ask in verse 20, who can stand in the presence of the LORD, this holy God, and their answer is to move the ark somewhere else. Deuteronomy 10:12 puts the same word at the head of what God requires, and Proverbs 1:7 calls it the beginning of knowledge. It is not a feeling about God; it is an accurate estimate of Him.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Philistines send the ark of the LORD back to Israel with gold guilt offerings; the ark travels straight to Beth Shemesh, where the people rejoice but God strikes down seventy of them for looking inside it, prompting them to send it on to Kiriath Jearim.

stories.title: 📦 1 Samuel 7
summaryBullets: Then the men of Kiriath-jearim came for the ark of the LORD and took it into Abinadab’s house on the hill. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD. (7:1).
And from that day a long time passed, twenty years in all, as the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim. And all the house of Israel mournfully sought the LORD. (7:2).

Then Samuel said to all the house of Israel, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among you, prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only. And He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.” (7:3).
So the Israelites put away the Baals and Ashtoreths and served only the LORD. (7:4).
Then Samuel said, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD on your behalf.” (7:5).

When they had gathered at Mizpah, they drew water and poured it out before the LORD. On that day they fasted, and there they confessed, “We have sinned against the LORD.” And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah. (7:6).
When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, their rulers marched up toward Israel. And when the Israelites learned of this, they feared the Philistines (7:7).
and said to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines.” (7:8).
Then Samuel took a suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. He cried out to the LORD on behalf of Israel, and the LORD answered him. (7:9).

As the Philistines drew near to fight against Israel, Samuel was offering up the burnt offering. But that day the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel. (7:10).
Then the men of Israel charged out of Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down all the way to an area below Beth-car. (7:11).
Afterward, Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He named it Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” (7:12).
So the Philistines were subdued, and they stopped invading the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. (7:13).

The cities from Ekron to Gath, which the Philistines had taken, were restored to Israel, who also delivered the surrounding territory from the hand of the Philistines. And there was peace between the Israelites and the Amorites. (7:14).
So Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. (7:15).
Every year he would go on a circuit from Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah, judging Israel in all these places. (7:16).
Then he would return to Ramah because his home was there, and there he judged Israel and built an altar to the LORD. (7:17).
crossRefs: Judges 10:15-16: Israel puts away the foreign gods and serves the LORD, and He can bear their misery no longer.
Genesis 35:2-4: Jacob tells his household to put away the foreign gods, and buries them under the oak at Shechem.
Deuteronomy 6:13-15: Fear the LORD your God, serve Him, swear by His name, and do not go after the gods of the peoples around you.
Exodus 14:24-25: The LORD throws the Egyptian army into a panic and clogs their chariot wheels so they drive heavily.
Joshua 4:4-9: Twelve stones are set up as a memorial so that later generations will ask what they mean.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר (Even ha-Ezer), stone of help
translationNotes.note: Verse 12 has Samuel set up a stone and name it, saying thus far the LORD has helped us. Setting up a single upright stone was the ordinary way of fixing an event to a place where almost nobody could read: Jacob does it at Bethel (Genesis 28:18), Joshua at Shechem (Joshua 24:26-27). The name carries an edge, because a place called Ebenezer is where Israel had camped when the ark was captured twenty years earlier (4:1, 5:1).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוּב (shuv), to turn back - Greek (LXX): ἐπιστρέφω (epistrepho)
translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word is not about feeling sorry; it is the plain verb for turning round and going back the way you came, used of a traveller, an army or a runaway. Verse 3 spells out what it involves in practice: if you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods from among you, direct your hearts to Him, and serve Him only. Verse 4 records them doing it. The word is an action first and an emotion afterwards, if at all.

translationNotes.term: Poured out water before the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיִּשְׁפְּכוּ (vayyishpekhu), and they poured out
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 pairs three things at Mizpah: they drew water and poured it out before the LORD, they fasted that day, and they said we have sinned against the LORD. Nothing in the law commands this, and it appears nowhere else in exactly this form; the nearest parallels are David pouring out to the LORD the water three men risked their lives to fetch (2 Samuel 23:16) and Lamentations 2:19, pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord. The text reports the act and leaves it standing.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְסָבַב (ve-savav), and he went around
translationNotes.note: Verses 15 to 17 describe a working legal system. Year by year Samuel travelled a fixed round, Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah, hearing cases in each, then came home to Ramah, where he judged as well and where he built an altar. That is a judge in the ordinary sense of the word, a circuit magistrate, which is not what most of the men in the book of Judges were. Samuel is the last of the judges and the only one who does the job that way.

Verses 3 and 4 have Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth. Ashtoreth is the goddess Astarte, worshipped from Canaan to Phoenicia as the power behind fertility and war, and her worship involved sexual rites at the shrine. Solomon later built a high place for Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians (1 Kings 11:5), and the Philistines put Saul's armour in her temple (1 Samuel 31:10).

stories.keyTakeaway: Israel repents of idol worship and gathers at Mizpah; when the Philistines attack, Samuel offers a sacrifice and the LORD defeats them with thunder, breaking Philistine power. Samuel sets up a memorial stone called Ebenezer and leads Israel as judge from multiple cities for the rest of his life.

stories.title: 👑 1 Samuel 8
summaryBullets: When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel. (8:1).
The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second was Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba. (8:2).
But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice. (8:3).
So all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah. (8:4).
“Look,” they said, “you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.” (8:5).
But when they said, “Give us a king to judge us,” their demand was displeasing in the sight of Samuel; so he prayed to the LORD. (8:6).
And the LORD said to Samuel, “Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king. (8:7).
Just as they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you. (8:8).
Now listen to their voice; but you must solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them.” (8:9).
So Samuel spoke all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking him for a king. (8:10).
He said, “This will be the manner of the king who will reign over you: He will take your sons and appoint them to serve his own chariots and horses, and to run in front of his chariots. (8:11).
He will appoint some for himself as commanders of thousands and of fifties, and others to plow his ground, to reap his harvest, and to make his weapons of war and equipment for his chariots. (8:12).
And he will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers. (8:13).
He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants. (8:14).
He will take a tenth of your grain and grape harvest and give it to his officials and servants. (8:15).
And he will take your menservants and maidservants and your best cattle and donkeys and put them to his own use. (8:16).
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves. (8:17).
When that day comes, you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day.” (8:18).
Nevertheless , the people refused to listen to Samuel. “No!” they said. “We must have a king over us. (8:19).
Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” (8:20).
Samuel listened to all the words of the people and repeated them in the hearing of the LORD. (8:21).
“Listen to their voice,” the LORD said to Samuel. “Appoint a king for them.” Then Samuel told the men of Israel, “Everyone must go back to his city.” (8:22).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 17:14-20: When you say, I will set a king over me like all the nations, here is the law that king must keep.
Judges 8:22-23: Gideon refuses to rule over Israel and tells them the LORD will rule over them.
1 Samuel 12:16-19: Samuel calls down thunder and rain in the wheat harvest, and Israel admits that asking for a king was evil.
Hosea 13:10-11: Where now is your king to save you? I gave you a king in My anger and took him away in My wrath.
1 Kings 12:1-16: Rehoboam promises a heavier yoke, and the tribes answer, what portion do we have in David.

translationNotes.note: Verse 4 brings the elders of Israel to Samuel at Ramah, and the name simply means the high place, a common name for a hilltop town. This one is in the hill country of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, and it is Samuel's base for his whole life: his parents' home (1:19), the town he returns to after every circuit and where he builds an altar (7:17), and where he is buried and mourned by all Israel (25:1). Jeremiah 31:15 has Rachel weeping in Ramah for her children.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שֹׁחַד (shochad), a bribe - בֶּצַע (betsa), dishonest gain
translationNotes.note: Verses 2 and 3 give the failure precisely. Samuel posted his two sons as judges at Beersheba, at the far southern edge of the country, a long way from Ramah and from him, and they turned aside after dishonest gain, took bribes and perverted judgment. The law names the offence twice and gives the reason: Exodus 23:8 and Deuteronomy 16:19 both say a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous. This is the grievance the elders build their demand on.

translationNotes.term: A king like all the nations
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כְּכָל־הַגּוֹיִם (ke-khol ha-goyim), like all the nations
translationNotes.note: The phrase in verses 5 and 20 is quoted from the law. Deuteronomy 17:14-20 had already foreseen Israel saying I will set a king over me like all the nations around me, and had set the terms: he must be one the LORD chooses and an Israelite; he must not multiply horses or send people back to Egypt for them; he must not multiply wives or silver and gold; and he must write out a copy of the law for himself and read it all his life. The request is not the problem the law names. The reason given for it in verse 20, so that we may be like the other nations, is.

Verses 11 to 18 are not a threat but a description of how monarchy actually ran in the ancient Near East: conscription of sons for chariots and armies, of daughters for the palace kitchens, a tenth of grain and flocks, and seizure of the best fields for royal officers. Every item on Samuel's list is attested in the administrative records of neighbouring kingdoms. The people hear it and still say, we will have a king.

stories.keyTakeaway: Samuel's corrupt sons prompt Israel's elders to demand a king like other nations; Samuel warns them of the king's oppressive claims, but they refuse to listen, and God tells Samuel to grant their request.

stories.title: 👑 1 Samuel 9
summaryBullets: Now there was a Benjamite, a powerful man, whose name was Kish son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah of Benjamin. (9:1).
And he had a son named Saul, choice and handsome, without equal among the Israelites — a head taller than any of the people. (9:2).
One day the donkeys of Saul’s father Kish wandered off, and Kish said to his son Saul, “Take one of the servants and go look for the donkeys.” (9:3).

So Saul passed through the hill country of Ephraim and then through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find the donkeys. He and the servant went through the region of Shaalim, but they were not there. Then they went through the land of Benjamin, and still they did not find them. (9:4).
When they reached the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant, “Come, let us go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us.” (9:5).
“Look,” said the servant, “in this city there is a man of God who is highly respected; everything he says surely comes to pass. Let us go there now. Perhaps he will tell us which way to go.” (9:6).
“If we do go,” Saul replied, “what can we give the man? For the bread in our packs is gone, and there is no gift to take to the man of God. What do we have?” (9:7).
The servant answered him again. “Look,” he said, “I have here in my hand a quarter shekel of silver. I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way.” (9:8).
(Formerly in Israel, a man on his way to inquire of God would say, “Come, let us go to the seer.” For the prophet of today was formerly called the seer.) (9:9).
“Good,” said Saul to his servant. “Come, let us go.” So they set out for the city where the man of God was. (9:10).
And as they were climbing the hill to the city, they met some young women coming out to draw water and asked, “Is the seer here?” (9:11).
“Yes, he is ahead of you,” they answered. “Hurry now, for today he has come to the city because the people have a sacrifice on the high place. (9:12).

As soon as you enter the city, you will find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice; after that, the guests will eat. Go up at once; you will find him.” (9:13).
So Saul and his servant went up toward the city, and as they were entering it, there was Samuel coming toward them on his way up to the high place. (9:14).
Now on the day before Saul’s arrival, the LORD had revealed to Samuel, (9:15).

“At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you are to anoint him ruler over My people Israel; he will save them from the hand of the Philistines. For I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me.” (9:16).
When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, “Here is the man of whom I spoke; he shall rule over My people.” (9:17).
Saul approached Samuel in the gateway and asked, “Would you please tell me where the seer’s house is?” (9:18).
“I am the seer,” Samuel replied. “Go up before me to the high place, for you shall eat with me today. And when I send you off in the morning, I will tell you all that is in your heart. (9:19).
As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found. And upon whom is all the desire of Israel, if not upon you and all your father’s house?” (9:20).
Saul replied, “Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? So why would you say such a thing to me?” (9:21).
Then Samuel took Saul and his servant, brought them into the hall, and seated them in the place of honor among those who were invited — about thirty in all. (9:22).
And Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you and told you to set aside.” (9:23).

So the cook picked up the leg and what was attached to it and set it before Saul. Then Samuel said, “Here is what was kept back. It was set apart for you. Eat, for it has been kept for you for this occasion, from the time I said, ‘I have invited the people.’” So Saul dined with Samuel that day. (9:24).
And after they had come down from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof of his house. (9:25).

They got up early in the morning, and just before dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, “Get ready, and I will send you on your way!” So Saul got ready, and both he and Samuel went outside together. (9:26).

As they were going down to the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell the servant to go on ahead of us, but you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God.” So the servant went on. (9:27).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 10:20-24: Saul is taken by lot at Mizpah and stands a head taller than any of the people.
1 Chronicles 29:29: The acts of David are written in the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the seer.
Leviticus 7:32-34: The right thigh of the peace offering is the priest's portion, the piece set before Saul at the meal.
Deuteronomy 12:2-4,13-14: Israel is to tear down the high places of the nations and sacrifice only at the place the LORD chooses.
1 Samuel 3:19-21: All Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רֹאֶה (roeh), one who sees - נָבִיא (navi), prophet
translationNotes.note: Verse 9 stops the story to explain an old word to a later reader: the man now called a prophet used to be called the seer. Roeh comes from the plain verb to see, and a related word, chozeh, is used of Gad, David's seer (2 Samuel 24:11). Verses 6 to 10 show what people expected of one, and it is very ordinary: two men who have lost their father's donkeys expect the man of God to tell them where to look, and the servant has a quarter shekel of silver ready as the fee.

A bamah is a raised open-air worship site with an altar, often on a hill above a town, reached by a stair or a path; verses 12 to 14 and 19 and 25 have Samuel presiding over a sacrifice at one and eating there in a hall. Before the temple was built this was normal and unremarkable, and 1 Kings 3:2-4 says so plainly, noting that Solomon himself sacrificed at the great high place at Gibeon. Afterwards the same word becomes the standing charge against nearly every king of Judah, because the sacrifice was supposed to be in one place only.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שׁוֹק (shoq), the thigh or leg
translationNotes.note: Verses 23 and 24 look like a small courtesy and are not. The right thigh of a peace offering was the portion the law gave to the officiating priest (Leviticus 7:32-33), and Samuel had it deliberately held back and set in front of Saul in the sight of about thirty invited guests. Serving a man the priest's own portion at a sacrificial meal marks him out in public before a word about kingship has been said.

translationNotes.term: A head taller than any of the people
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשִּׁכְמוֹ וָמַעְלָה (mi-shikhmo va-malah), from his shoulders upward
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 introduces Saul by his appearance and his height, and 10:23 repeats it when he is presented to the nation. Size was a real qualification for a war leader in a period when battles were decided by men standing in line with hand weapons, and the crowd's reaction in 10:24 shows they took it as one. Chapter 16:7 answers this verse directly when Samuel is sent to Bethlehem and told that man looks at the outward appearance but the LORD looks at the heart.

Both a weight (about 0.4 oz / 11 g) and a currency unit. In Old Testament economy a common laborer earned roughly half a shekel per month, so the 20 shekels paid for Joseph (Genesis 37:28) was about three years of wages. The temple tax was half a shekel (Exodus 30:13); in New Testament reckoning that equaled two denarii / two days' wages.

stories.keyTakeaway: Saul searches for his father's lost donkeys and meets the prophet Samuel, who has been told by God that Saul will become ruler over Israel; Samuel invites him to eat and says the donkeys have been found, then asks to speak with him alone the next morning.

stories.title: 👑 1 Samuel 10
summaryBullets: Then Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul’s head, kissed him, and said, “Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance? (10:1).

When you leave me today, you will find two men at Rachel’s tomb in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin. They will say to you, ‘The donkeys you seek have been found, and now your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and started worrying about you, asking, “What should I do about my son?”’ (10:2).

Then you will go on from there until you come to the Oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. (10:3).
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands. (10:4).

After that you will come to Gibeah of God, where the Philistines have an outpost. As you approach the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place, preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres, and they will be prophesying. (10:5).
Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them; and you will be transformed into a different person. (10:6).
When these signs have come, do as the occasion demands, for God is with you. (10:7).

And you shall go before me to Gilgal, and surely I will come to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.” (10:8).
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul’s heart, and all the signs came to pass that day. (10:9).
When Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, a group of prophets met him. Then the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied along with them. (10:10).
When all those who had formerly known Saul saw him prophesying with the prophets, they asked one another, “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?” (10:11).
Then a man who lived there replied, “And who is their father?” So the saying became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (10:12).
And when Saul had finished prophesying, he went up to the high place. (10:13).
Now Saul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you go?” “To look for the donkeys,” Saul replied. “When we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel.” (10:14).
“Tell me,” Saul’s uncle asked, “what did Samuel say to you?” (10:15).
And Saul replied, “He assured us that the donkeys had been found.” But Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship. (10:16).
After this, Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah (10:17).

and said to the Israelites, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I rescued you from the hands of the Egyptians and of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’ (10:18).

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and afflictions, and you have said to Him, ‘No, set a king over us.’ Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and clans.” (10:19).
Thus Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected. (10:20).

Then he had the tribe of Benjamin come forward by its clans, and the clan of Matri was selected. Finally, Saul son of Kish was selected. But when they looked for him, they could not find him. (10:21).
So again they inquired of the LORD, “Has the man come here yet?” And the LORD replied, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.” (10:22).
So they ran and brought Saul, and when he stood among the people, he was a head taller than any of the others. (10:23).
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “Long live the king!” (10:24).
Then Samuel explained to the people the rights of kingship. He wrote them on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD. And Samuel sent all the people away, each to his own home. (10:25).
Saul also went to his home in Gibeah, and the men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him. (10:26).
But some worthless men said, “How can this man save us?” So they despised him and brought him no gifts; but Saul remained silent about it. (10:27).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 16:13: Samuel anoints David with the horn of oil, and the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon him from that day.
Numbers 11:24-29: The Spirit rests on seventy elders and they prophesy, and Moses wishes all the LORD's people were prophets.
Deuteronomy 17:18-20: The king writes for himself a copy of this law, the practice behind the book Samuel writes in verse 25.
Joshua 7:14-18: Israel is brought near by tribe, by clan, and by household until Achan is taken by lot.
Genesis 35:19-20: Rachel dies on the way to Ephrath and Jacob sets a pillar on her grave, the tomb in Saul's first sign.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: פַּךְ הַשֶּׁמֶן (pakh ha-shemen), the flask of oil - מָשִׁיחַ (mashiach), anointed one
translationNotes.note: Verse 1 has Samuel pour oil on Saul's head from a small flask and kiss him. Pouring perfumed olive oil over the head was how a man was installed in an office set apart by God: priests in Exodus 29:7, and kings from here onward. The man so treated is called the LORD's mashiach, His anointed, which comes into English through Greek as Messiah and Christ. This first anointing is done privately, with no witness but the two of them, and only in verse 24 does the nation get told.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶבֶל נְבִיאִים (chevel neviim), a band of prophets
translationNotes.note: Verses 5, 10 and 11 describe bands of prophets attached to a sanctuary, coming down from the high place in procession with harp, tambourine, flute and lyre, prophesying together. Music and prophecy went together: Elisha calls for a musician before the word comes to him (2 Kings 3:15), and David sets Levites apart to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals (1 Chronicles 25:1). Groups like this appear again around Samuel at Ramah (19:20) and around Elijah and Elisha as the sons of the prophets (2 Kings 2:3-7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיִּלָּכֵד (vayyillakhed), and he was taken
translationNotes.note: Verses 20 and 21 narrow the whole nation down in three steps, tribe, then clan, then man, by lot in front of everyone. Saul has already been anointed in private in verse 1, so this is not how the choice is made but how it is proved; nobody can say the prophet picked his own candidate. The same procedure finds Achan in Joshua 7:16-18. The man it lands on is found hiding among the baggage.

translationNotes.term: The rights and duties of kingship
translationNotes.note: Verse 25 has Samuel set out the terms of the office, write them on a scroll and lay it up before the LORD. The king is put under a written document from the first day, deposited at the sanctuary where he does not control it. Deuteronomy 17:18-20 requires the king to write himself a copy of the law and read it all his days so that his heart is not lifted above his brothers. Israel gets a monarchy with a text over it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּנֵי בְלִיַּעַל (bene beliyyaal), sons of worthlessness
translationNotes.note: Beliyyaal is a compound meaning without profit or without worth, and the phrase brands a man as good for nothing rather than merely badly behaved. Scripture uses it of Eli's sons robbing the altar (2:12), of Nabal (25:17, 25), of the men of Gibeah (Judges 19:22), and here in verse 27 of those who ask how can this man save us. By the first century the word had hardened into a name for the evil one, which is how Paul uses Belial at 2 Corinthians 6:15.

stories.keyTakeaway: Samuel anoints Saul as king with oil and describes signs that will confirm God's choice; all the signs occur that day. Samuel then assembles Israel at Mizpah, selects Saul by lot, and presents him to the people as their chosen king, though some despise him.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 11
summaryBullets: Then Nahash the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to him, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.” (11:1).
But Nahash the Ammonite replied, “I will make a treaty with you on one condition, that I may put out everyone’s right eye and bring reproach upon all Israel.” (11:2).
“Hold off for seven days,” replied the elders of Jabesh, “and let us send messengers throughout Israel. If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you.” (11:3).
When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and relayed these words in the hearing of the people, they all wept aloud. (11:4).
Just then Saul was returning from the field, behind his oxen. “What troubles the people?” asked Saul. “Why are they weeping?” And they relayed to him the words of the men from Jabesh. (11:5).
When Saul heard their words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger. (11:6).

He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them by messengers throughout the land of Israel, proclaiming, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” Then the terror of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out together as one man. (11:7).
And when Saul numbered them at Bezek, there were 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah. (11:8).

So they said to the messengers who had come, “Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead: ‘Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.’” And when the messengers relayed this to the men of Jabesh, they rejoiced. (11:9).
Then the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you.” (11:10).

The next day Saul organized the troops into three divisions, and during the morning watch they invaded the camp of the Ammonites and slaughtered them, until the hottest part of the day. And the survivors were so scattered that no two of them were left together. (11:11).
Then the people said to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Bring those men here so we can kill them!” (11:12).
But Saul ordered, “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.” (11:13).
Then Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.” (11:14).

So all the people went to Gilgal and confirmed Saul as king in the presence of the LORD. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly. (11:15).
crossRefs: Judges 19:29-30: The Levite cuts the body into twelve pieces and sends them through all the territory of Israel to summon the tribes.
Judges 21:8-14: Jabesh-gilead is struck for not coming up to Mizpah, and its young women are given to the survivors of Benjamin.
Judges 11:4-33: Jephthah's war with the Ammonites over the land east of the Jordan.
1 Samuel 31:11-13: The men of Jabesh-gilead march all night to take Saul's body down from the wall of Beth-shan.
Deuteronomy 23:3-6: No Ammonite is to enter the assembly of the LORD, even to the tenth generation.

translationNotes.note: Verse 13 has Saul say the LORD has worked salvation in Israel today, and the thing he is describing is the lifting of a siege. Yeshuah in the Old Testament means rescue from a concrete danger, an enemy army, an illness, a court case, and the same word supplies the names Joshua and Jesus, both meaning the LORD saves. Understanding it as a physical deliverance first is what lets a reader hear it correctly everywhere else it appears.

Jabesh-gilead lies east of the Jordan in Gilead, cut off from the western tribes by the river. Two older facts explain the whole chapter. The town had been destroyed by the other tribes for staying away from the assembly, and its four hundred surviving young women were given to the men of Benjamin as wives (Judges 21:8-14), so Saul the Benjaminite is answering a call from his own mother's kin. Verse 3 shows the ordinary law of siege in that world: a town could ask for a set number of days to seek relief, and surrender if none came.

Nahash offers terms in verse 2 that would leave every man in Jabesh alive but blind in the right eye. A soldier held his shield on the left arm, which covered the left eye, so a man who lost the right eye could no longer fight in a line. Josephus states that purpose plainly in his account of the siege (Antiquities 6.5.1). It was a surrender that turned a town into permanent non-combatants and a standing disgrace to Israel.

Verse 7 has Saul cut a yoke of oxen apart and send the pieces through Israel with a threat against anyone who does not come out. The same summons is used once before, in Judges 19:29, and it was understood: the pieces stood for what would happen to the man's own herd, and the messenger who carried them was calling a muster nobody could pretend not to have received.

stories.keyTakeaway: Nahash besieges Jabesh Gilead and demands to gouge out the right eye of its men; Saul musters Israel, crushes the Ammonites in a night attack, and is publicly confirmed as king at Gilgal.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 12
summaryBullets: Then Samuel said to all Israel, “I have listened to your voice in all that you have said to me, and I have set over you a king. (12:1).
Now here is the king walking before you, and I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day. (12:2).

Here I am. Bear witness against me before the LORD and before His anointed: Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes? Tell me, and I will restore it to you.” (12:3).
“You have not cheated us or oppressed us,” they replied, “nor have you taken anything from the hand of man.” (12:4).
Samuel said to them, “The LORD is a witness against you, and His anointed is a witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand.” “He is a witness,” they replied. (12:5).
Then Samuel said to the people, “The LORD is the One who appointed Moses and Aaron, and who brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. (12:6).
Now present yourselves, so that I may confront you before the LORD with all the righteous acts He has done for you and your fathers. (12:7).
When Jacob went to Egypt, your fathers cried out to the LORD, and He sent them Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them in this place. (12:8).

But they forgot the LORD their God, and He sold them into the hand of Sisera the commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hands of the Philistines and the king of Moab, who fought against them. (12:9).

Then they cried out to the LORD and said, ‘We have sinned, for we have forsaken the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths. Now deliver us from the hands of our enemies, that we may serve You.’ (12:10).
So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and He delivered you from the hands of your enemies on every side, and you dwelt securely. (12:11).
But when you saw that Nahash king of the Ammonites was moving against you, you said to me, ‘No, we must have a king to rule over us’— even though the LORD your God was your king. (12:12).
Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you requested. Behold, the LORD has placed a king over you. (12:13).

If you fear the LORD and serve Him and obey His voice, and if you do not rebel against the command of the LORD, and if both you and the king who rules over you follow the LORD your God, then all will be well. (12:14).
But if you disobey the LORD and rebel against His command, then the hand of the LORD will be against you as it was against your fathers. (12:15).
Now, therefore, present yourselves and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes. (12:16).

Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain, so that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king.” (12:17).
So Samuel called to the LORD, and on that day the LORD sent thunder and rain. As a result, all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel. (12:18).
They pleaded with Samuel, “Pray to the LORD your God for your servants so that we will not die! For we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king.” (12:19).
“Do not be afraid,” Samuel replied. “Even though you have committed all this evil, do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart. (12:20).
Do not turn aside after worthless things that cannot profit you or deliver you, for they are empty. (12:21).
Indeed, for the sake of His great name, the LORD will not abandon His people, because He was pleased to make you His own. (12:22).
As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. And I will continue to teach you the good and right way. (12:23).
Above all, fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all your heart; consider what great things He has done for you. (12:24).
But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away.” (12:25).
crossRefs: Numbers 16:15: Moses says he has not taken one donkey from them and has not wronged any one of them.
Acts 20:33-35: Paul says he coveted no one's silver, gold, or clothing, and worked with his own hands.
Judges 2:11-19: The repeating pattern of forsaking the LORD, being sold into enemy hands, crying out, and being delivered by a judge.
Deuteronomy 11:13-17: If you obey, He gives the rain in its season; if you turn aside, He shuts up the heavens and there is no rain.
Proverbs 26:1: Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, honour is not fitting for a fool.

translationNotes.note: Verses 3 to 5 are a formal audit, not a burst of feeling.
