A judge leaving office stands in front of the people and invites any claim against him: whose ox or donkey have I taken, whom have I defrauded, from whose hand have I taken a bribe. The people are then made to answer on the record, and verse 5 seals it with the LORD as witness and the newly made king as witness, and their reply, he is witness. Samuel hands over with his accounts formally closed.

This chapter uses the phrase at both ends of its range within a few verses. In verse 18 the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel when thunder came out of a clear harvest sky, which is fright. In verse 24 Samuel tells them to fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all their heart, which is a settled way of living. Deuteronomy 10:12 puts the same word first in the list of what God requires, and Proverbs 1:7 makes it the beginning of knowledge.

Verses 9 to 11 run through the pattern of the book of Judges in three sentences: Israel forgot the LORD, He sold them into the hand of Sisera, of the Philistines and of the king of Moab, they cried out, and He sent deliverers. The men listed are Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, then Barak, then Jephthah, then Samuel himself. He puts his own name last in the list, which is how he closes the era before handing the country to a king.

Israel's rain falls from about October to April, and the wheat harvest in May and June is reliably dry; that is when threshing floors are in use and a downpour ruins the crop on the ground. Samuel calls for thunder and rain at exactly the season when nobody had ever seen it, which is why verse 18 says the people greatly feared. Proverbs 26:1 uses the same impossibility as a byword.

stories.keyTakeaway: Samuel vindicated his leadership before all Israel, then recounted God's faithfulness through the judges before warning that blessing depends on obedience to the LORD and the new king. When the people fear the thunder and rain Samuel called down, he reassures them that God will not reject his people if they serve faithfully.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 13
summaryBullets: Saul was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel forty-two years. (13:1).

He chose for himself three thousand men of Israel: Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. And the rest of the troops he sent away, each to his own home. (13:2).
Then Jonathan attacked the Philistine outpost at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. So Saul blew the ram’s horn throughout the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear!” (13:3).
And all Israel heard the news: “Saul has attacked an outpost of the Philistines, and now Israel has become a stench to the Philistines!” Then the people were summoned to join Saul at Gilgal. (13:4).

Now the Philistines assembled to fight against Israel with three thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and troops as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven. (13:5).
Seeing that they were in danger because their troops were hard-pressed, the men of Israel hid in caves and thickets, among the rocks, and in cellars and cisterns. (13:6).
Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan into the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul, however, remained at Gilgal, and all his troops were quaking in fear. (13:7).
And Saul waited seven days for the time appointed by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the troops began to desert Saul. (13:8).
So he said, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” And he offered up the burnt offering. (13:9).
Just as he finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived, and Saul went out to greet him. (13:10).

“What have you done?” Samuel asked. And Saul replied, “When I saw that the troops were deserting me, and that you did not come at the appointed time and the Philistines were gathering at Michmash, (13:11).
I thought, ‘Now the Philistines will descend upon me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.’ So I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering.” (13:12).

“You have acted foolishly,” Samuel declared. “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you; if you had, the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel for all time. (13:13).
But now your kingdom will not endure; the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people, because you have not kept the command of the LORD.” (13:14).
Then Samuel set out from Gilgal and went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. And Saul numbered the troops who were with him, about six hundred men. (13:15).
Now Saul and Jonathan his son and the troops with them were staying in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash. (13:16).
And raiders went out of the Philistine camp in three divisions. One headed toward Ophrah in the land of Shual, (13:17).
another toward Beth-horon, and the third down the border road overlooking the Valley of Zeboim facing the wilderness. (13:18).
And no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” (13:19).
Instead, all the Israelites would go down to the Philistines to sharpen their plowshares, mattocks, axes, and sickles. (13:20).
The charge was a pim for sharpening a plowshare or mattock, a third of a shekel for sharpening a pitchfork or an axe, and a third of a shekel for repointing an oxgoad. (13:21).
So on the day of battle not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan; only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. (13:22).
And a garrison of the Philistines had gone out to the pass at Michmash. (13:23).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 10:8: Samuel tells Saul to go down to Gilgal and wait seven days until he comes to offer the sacrifices.
Numbers 18:1-7: Only Aaron and his sons may do the work of the priesthood; any outsider who comes near is to be put to death.
1 Samuel 15:22-23: To obey is better than sacrifice, and rebellion is as the sin of divination.
Acts 13:22: God removed Saul and raised up David, a man after His own heart, who will do all My will.
Judges 5:8: Was shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel, in the days when they chose new gods.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֹלָה (olah), that which goes up - Greek (LXX): ὁλοκαύτωμα (holokautoma)
translationNotes.note: The olah is the offering burned entire, with nothing kept back for the priest or the worshipper to eat, and the name means the thing that goes up in smoke. Before a battle it was normal to offer one, which is what Saul is waiting seven days at Gilgal to have Samuel do (10:8). Verses 9 to 12 have him call for it and offer it himself as the army melts away, and Samuel arrives as he finishes. The Greek word behind it gives English holocaust.

translationNotes.term: A man after His own heart
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כִּלְבָבוֹ (kilvavo), according to his heart
translationNotes.note: Samuel's sentence in verse 14 says the LORD has sought out for Himself a man according to His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people. In Hebrew the heart is where a person decides, not where he feels; it is closer to the mind and the will than to the emotions. The phrase describes a man whose choices line up with God's, and the chapter has just shown Saul making the opposite kind. Paul quotes the line at Acts 13:22.

Verses 19 to 22 report that the Philistines allowed no smith in Israel, so farmers had to go down to them to sharpen a ploughshare, mattock, axe, or sickle, and only Saul and Jonathan had a sword or spear. Controlling ironworking was how the coastal cities kept the hill country disarmed; Israel could farm but could not arm. Judges 1:19 gives the other half of the picture, iron chariots the highlanders could not face.

Verse 21 gives the Philistine sharpening charge as a pim. The word appears nowhere else in Scripture and nobody knew what it meant until inscribed stone weights marked pym were dug up in Judah in the early twentieth century. A pim weighs about 7.8 grams, roughly two thirds of a shekel, so the fee for putting an edge on a farm tool was two thirds of the standard silver unit, charged per tool.

A town about seven miles northeast of Jerusalem, on the north lip of the Wadi Suweinit, a steep gorge that cuts the road running east from the central ridge. Michmash sits on one side and Geba on the other, with the ravine between them, so an army holding Michmash sealed the pass. That gorge is the ground of Jonathan's climb in the next chapter.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jonathan strikes a Philistine outpost, prompting Saul to gather troops, but the Philistines assemble a vastly superior force that terrifies the Israelites into hiding. Saul offers a burnt offering without waiting for Samuel, who arrives to condemn him for disobeying the LORD's command and announces that his kingdom will not endure.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 14
summaryBullets: One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man bearing his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the Philistine outpost on the other side.” But Jonathan did not tell his father. (14:1).
Meanwhile, Saul was staying under the pomegranate tree in Migron on the outskirts of Gibeah. And the troops who were with him numbered about six hundred men, (14:2).

including Ahijah, who was wearing an ephod. He was the son of Ichabod’s brother Ahitub son of Phinehas, the son of Eli the priest of the LORD in Shiloh. But the troops did not know that Jonathan had left. (14:3).
Now there were cliffs on both sides of the pass that Jonathan intended to cross to reach the Philistine outpost. One was named Bozez and the other Seneh. (14:4).
One cliff stood to the north toward Michmash, and the other to the south toward Geba. (14:5).

Jonathan said to the young man bearing his armor, “Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will work on our behalf. Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few.” (14:6).
His armor-bearer replied, “Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you heart and soul.” (14:7).
“Very well,” said Jonathan, “we will cross over toward these men and show ourselves to them. (14:8).
If they say, ‘Wait until we come to you,’ then we will stay where we are and will not go up to them. (14:9).
But if they say, ‘Come on up,’ then we will go up, because this will be our sign that the LORD has delivered them into our hands.” (14:10).
So the two of them showed themselves to the outpost of the Philistines, who exclaimed, “Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the holes in which they were hiding!” (14:11).

So the men of the outpost called out to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, “Come on up, and we will teach you a lesson!” “Follow me,” Jonathan told his armor-bearer, “for the LORD has delivered them into the hand of Israel.” (14:12).
So Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. And the Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer followed and finished them off. (14:13).
In that first assault, Jonathan and his armor-bearer struck down about twenty men in about half an acre of land. (14:14).

Then panic struck the Philistines in the camp, in the field, and among all the people. Even those in the outposts and raiding parties trembled. Indeed, the earth quaked, and panic spread from God. (14:15).
Now when Saul’s watchmen at Gibeah in Benjamin looked and saw the troops melting away and scattering in every direction, (14:16).
Saul said to the troops who were with him, “Call the roll and see who has left us.” And when they had called the roll, they saw that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there. (14:17).
Then Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ark of God.” (For at that time it was with the Israelites.) (14:18).
While Saul was talking to the priest, the commotion in the Philistine camp continued to increase. So Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hand.” (14:19).
Then Saul and all his troops assembled and marched to the battle, and they found the Philistines in total confusion, with each man wielding the sword against his neighbor. (14:20).
And the Hebrews who had previously gone up into the surrounding camps to join the Philistines now went over to the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. (14:21).
When all the Israelites who had been hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they also joined the battle in close pursuit. (14:22).
So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle moved on beyond Beth-aven. (14:23).

Now the men of Israel were in distress that day, for Saul had placed the troops under an oath, saying, “Cursed is the man who eats any food before evening, before I have taken vengeance on my enemies.” So none of the troops tasted any food. (14:24).
Then all the troops entered the forest, and there was honey on the ground. (14:25).
And when they entered the forest and saw the flowing honey, not one of them put his hand to his mouth, because they feared the oath. (14:26).

Jonathan, however, had not heard that his father had bound the people with the oath. So he reached out the end of the staff in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened. (14:27).
Then one of the soldiers told him, “Your father bound the troops with a solemn oath, saying, ‘Cursed is the man who eats food today.’ That is why the people are faint.” (14:28).
“My father has brought trouble to the land,” Jonathan replied. “Just look at how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey. (14:29).
How much better it would have been if the troops had eaten freely today from the plunder they took from their enemies! Would not the slaughter of the Philistines have been much greater?” (14:30).
That day, after the Israelites had struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, the people were very faint. (14:31).
So they rushed greedily to the plunder, taking sheep, cattle, and calves. They slaughtered them on the ground and ate meat with the blood still in it. (14:32).

Then someone reported to Saul: “Look, the troops are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it.” “You have broken faith,” said Saul. “Roll a large stone over here at once.” (14:33).

Then he said, “Go among the troops and tell them, ‘Each man must bring me his ox or his sheep, slaughter them in this place, and then eat. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with the blood still in it.’” So that night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there. (14:34).
Then Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD. (14:35).

And Saul said, “Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until dawn, leaving no man alive!” “Do what seems good to you,” the troops replied. But the priest said, “We must consult God here.” (14:36).
So Saul inquired of God, “Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will You give them into the hand of Israel?” But God did not answer him that day. (14:37).
Therefore Saul said, “Come here, all you leaders of the troops, and let us investigate how this sin has occurred today. (14:38).
As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives, even if it is my son Jonathan, he must die!” But not one of the troops said a word. (14:39).
Then Saul said to all Israel, “You stand on one side, and I and my son Jonathan will stand on the other side.” “Do what seems good to you,” the troops replied. (14:40).

So Saul said to the LORD, the God of Israel, “Why have You not answered Your servant this day? If the fault is with me or my son Jonathan, respond with Urim, but if the fault is with the men of Israel, respond with Thummim.” And Jonathan and Saul were selected, but the people were cleared of the charge. (14:41).
Then Saul said, “Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan.” And Jonathan was selected. (14:42).
“Tell me what you have done,” Saul commanded him. So Jonathan told him, “I only tasted a little honey with the end of the staff that was in my hand. And now I must die?” (14:43).
And Saul declared, “May God punish me, and ever so severely, if you, Jonathan, do not surely die!” (14:44).

But the people said to Saul, “Must Jonathan die — he who accomplished such a great deliverance for Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, for with God’s help he has accomplished this today.” So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die. (14:45).
Then Saul gave up his pursuit of the Philistines, and the Philistines returned to their own land. (14:46).

After Saul had assumed the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side — the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he routed them. (14:47).
He fought valiantly and defeated the Amalekites, delivering Israel from the hands of its plunderers. (14:48).
Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His two daughters were named Merab (his firstborn) and Michal (his younger daughter). (14:49).
His wife’s name was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The name of the commander of his army was Abner, the son of Saul’s uncle Ner. (14:50).
Saul’s father Kish and Abner’s father Ner were sons of Abiel. (14:51).
And the war with the Philistines was fierce for all the days of Saul. So whenever he noticed any strong or brave man, Saul would enlist him. (14:52).
crossRefs: Judges 7:1-8,16-22: Gideon's three hundred, cut down so Israel could not claim its own hand had saved it.
Leviticus 17:10-14: Anyone who eats blood will be cut off, for the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Deuteronomy 12:23-25: Be sure not to eat the blood, for the blood is the life; pour it out on the earth like water.
Numbers 27:21: Eleazar shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD.
Judges 11:30-39: Jephthah's rash vow and what it cost him when his daughter came out to meet him.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עַל־הַדָּם (al ha-dam), with the blood
translationNotes.note: Verses 32 to 34 have starving men fall on captured animals and eat them with the blood still in them, and Saul calls it treachery against the LORD. The rule is old and absolute: Genesis 9:4 gives it to Noah, and Leviticus 17:10-14 repeats it with the reason, that the life of the flesh is in the blood and God has given it for atonement on the altar. An animal had to be bled out on the ground and covered before it was eaten, and Saul rolls a great stone over for them to slaughter on properly.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: צֶמֶד (tsemed), a yoke of oxen
translationNotes.note: Verse 14 measures the ground the way a farmer would: the Hebrew reckons it as about half the strip a yoke of oxen ploughs, and half an acre is the translator's estimate of that. Fields were measured in work rather than in surveyed area, exactly as Isaiah 5:10 prices a vineyard at ten yoke, meaning ten days' ploughing for a pair. What the verse is saying is that two men killed twenty in a space smaller than one morning's furrow.

translationNotes.term: The oath that bound the army
translationNotes.note: Verse 24 puts the whole army under a curse against eating before evening, and the chapter then works out the cost of it: the men are faint, Jonathan eats honey without having heard the oath, God gives no answer when Saul asks, and the lot falls on Jonathan. Verse 45 is the crux. The army buys him back, and the Hebrew verb is padah, the ordinary word for redeeming a life by payment, so the men themselves ransom the king's son out from under the king's own oath.

Verses 4 and 5 name the two rock crags on either side of the Michmash gorge, one facing north toward Michmash and one south toward Geba. The wadi between them drops steeply, which is why verse 13 has Jonathan and his armour-bearer climbing up on hands and feet. Nobody watches a cliff, and two men coming over the lip where no army could come is what starts the panic.

Two objects kept in the fold of the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:30) and used to put a question to God that could be answered yes or no, or to single out one party from another. Verses 18 to 19 and 36 to 42 show the method in use: Saul asks, no answer comes, and then lots are cast between the people and Jonathan. They pass out of use after David's reign, and Ezra 2:63 records the returned exiles still waiting for a priest with Urim and Thummim.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jonathan and his armor-bearer attack a Philistine outpost and trigger a panic that leads Israel to victory, but Saul's oath forbidding food costs the army strength; when Jonathan unknowingly breaks the oath by eating honey, Saul condemns him to death until the troops intervene. The chapter ends by noting Saul's family and his ongoing battles against surrounding nations.

stories.title: ❌ 1 Samuel 15
summaryBullets: Then Samuel said to Saul, “The LORD sent me to anoint you king over His people Israel. Now therefore, listen to the words of the LORD. (15:1).
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘I witnessed what the Amalekites did to the Israelites when they opposed them on their way up from Egypt. (15:2).

Now go and attack the Amalekites and devote to destruction all that belongs to them. Do not spare them, but put to death men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.’” (15:3).
So Saul summoned the troops and numbered them at Telaim — 200,000 foot soldiers and 10,000 men of Judah. (15:4).
Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley. (15:5).

And he warned the Kenites, “Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt, go on and get away from the Amalekites. Otherwise I will sweep you away with them.” So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites. (15:6).
Then Saul struck down the Amalekites all the way from Havilah to Shur, which is east of Egypt. (15:7).
He captured Agag king of Amalek alive, but devoted all the others to destruction with the sword. (15:8).

Saul and his troops spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else. They were unwilling to devote them to destruction, but they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless. (15:9).
Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel, saying, (15:10).
“I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” And Samuel was distressed and cried out to the LORD all that night. (15:11).
Early in the morning Samuel got up to confront Saul, but he was told, “Saul has gone to Carmel, and behold, he has set up a monument for himself and has turned and gone down to Gilgal.” (15:12).
When Samuel reached him, Saul said to him, “May the LORD bless you. I have carried out the LORD’s instructions.” (15:13).
But Samuel replied, “Then what is this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle that I hear?” (15:14).
Saul answered, “The troops brought them from the Amalekites; they spared the best sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God, but the rest we devoted to destruction.” (15:15).
“Stop!” exclaimed Samuel. “Let me tell you what the LORD said to me last night.” “Tell me,” Saul replied. (15:16).
And Samuel said, “Although you were once small in your own eyes, have you not become the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel (15:17).
and sent you on a mission, saying, ‘Go and devote to destruction the sinful Amalekites. Fight against them until you have wiped them out.’ (15:18).
So why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush upon the plunder and do evil in the sight of the LORD?” (15:19).
“But I did obey the LORD,” Saul replied. “I went on the mission that the LORD gave me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek and devoted the Amalekites to destruction. (15:20).
The troops took sheep and cattle from the plunder, the best of the things devoted to destruction, in order to sacrifice them to the LORD your God at Gilgal.” (15:21).

But Samuel declared: “Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obedience to His voice? Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams. (15:22).
For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and arrogance is like the wickedness of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.” (15:23).
Then Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s commandment and your instructions, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice. (15:24).
Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me so I can worship the LORD.” (15:25).
“I will not return with you,” Samuel replied. “For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and He has rejected you as king over Israel.” (15:26).
As Samuel turned to go, Saul grabbed the hem of his robe, and it tore. (15:27).
So Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you. (15:28).
Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind.” (15:29).
“I have sinned,” Saul replied. “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel. Come back with me, so that I may worship the LORD your God.” (15:30).
So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD. (15:31).
Then Samuel said, “Bring me Agag king of the Amalekites.” Agag came to him cheerfully, for he thought, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.” (15:32).
But Samuel declared: “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women.” And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD at Gilgal. (15:33).
Then Samuel went to Ramah, but Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul. (15:34).
And to the day of his death, Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul, and the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel. (15:35).
crossRefs: Exodus 17:8-16: Amalek attacked Israel; God swore to blot them out.
Deuteronomy 25:17-19: Command to remember Amalek and erase them.
Hosea 6:6: 'I desire steadfast love, not sacrifice.'
Psalm 51:16-17: God delights in broken spirit over ritual.
Wisdom of Solomon 10:12: Wisdom delivered a righteous man in battle.

translationNotes.note: Ban of complete destruction, human and animal. Partial obedience (sparing Agag, animals) was rebellion.
Used of God in v.11 and v.29; paradox: God is grieved at human sin yet His purposes stand unchanged.
Lit. 'cut into pieces.' Brutal execution underscoring God’s judgment. Not softened; Samuel carried it out when Saul would not.

A nomadic raiding people of the Negev and Sinai, descended from Esau's grandson (Genesis 36:12). They attacked Israel's exhausted stragglers at the rear on the way out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 25:17-19), and God swore war with them from generation to generation (Exodus 17:14-16). The command in verse 3 is the execution of a sentence passed four hundred years earlier, not a new war.

Verse 6 has Saul warn the Kenites to move out from among the Amalekites before he strikes. They were the people of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law (Judges 1:16), who had travelled with Israel from Sinai and settled in the south of Judah. The warning is a debt being honoured, and it shows the ban in verse 3 was aimed at a specific people and not at everyone in the area.

stories.keyTakeaway: Saul spares Agag and animals against command. Samuel declares his rejection as king and executes Agag.

stories.title: 🛢️ 1 Samuel 16
summaryBullets: Now the LORD said to Samuel, “How long are you going to mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself.” (16:1).
“How can I go?” Samuel asked. “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” The LORD answered, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.’ (16:2).
Then invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I indicate.” (16:3).
So Samuel did what the LORD had said and went to Bethlehem. When the elders of the town met him, they trembled and asked, “Do you come in peace?” (16:4).

“In peace,” he replied. “I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” Then he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice. (16:5).
When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and said, “Surely here before the LORD is His anointed.” (16:6).

But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.” (16:7).
Then Jesse called Abinadab and presented him to Samuel, who said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” (16:8).
Next Jesse presented Shammah, but Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.” (16:9).
Thus Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel told him, “The LORD has not chosen any of these.” (16:10).

And Samuel asked him, “Are these all the sons you have?” “There is still the youngest,” Jesse replied, “but he is tending the sheep.” “Send for him,” Samuel replied. “For we will not sit down to eat until he arrives.” (16:11).
So Jesse sent for his youngest son and brought him in. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. And the LORD said, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one.” (16:12).
So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Then Samuel set out and went to Ramah. (16:13).
Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him. (16:14).
Saul’s servants said to him, “Surely a spirit of distress from God is tormenting you. (16:15).
Let our lord command your servants here to seek out someone who can skillfully play the harp. Whenever the spirit of distress from God is upon you, he is to play it, and you will be well.” (16:16).
And Saul commanded his servants, “Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me.” (16:17).

One of the servants answered, “I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp. He is a mighty man of valor, a warrior, eloquent and handsome, and the LORD is with him.” (16:18).
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, “Send me your son David, who is with the sheep.” (16:19).
And Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat and sent them to Saul with his son David. (16:20).
When David came to Saul and entered his service, Saul loved him very much, and David became his armor-bearer. (16:21).
Then Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him.” (16:22).
And whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would pick up his harp and play. Then Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would depart from him. (16:23).
crossRefs: Genesis 49:10: The scepter shall not depart from Judah (David from Judah’s line).
Ruth 4:18-22: Genealogy from Perez to Jesse, David’s father.
Psalm 78:70-72: God chose David from the sheepfolds.
1 Chronicles 2:13-15: Jesse’s sons listed; David the youngest.
Sirach 47:1-11: Praise of David’s anointing and Spirit-filled leadership.

translationNotes.note: Pouring oil to consecrate for office. From this root comes 'Messiah' (anointed one) and 'Christ' (Greek).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רוּחַ יְהוָה (ruaḥ YHWH); Greek: πνεῦμα Κυρίου (pneuma Kyriou)
translationNotes.note: God’s empowering presence. Here it rests on David permanently but departs from Saul.
Means 'evil/harmful spirit.' The text attributes Saul’s torment to God’s judgment, understood as affliction or oppression allowed by God.

stories.keyTakeaway: God sends Samuel to anoint David, the youngest son of Jesse. The Spirit rests on David, leaves Saul, and David enters Saul’s service with the lyre.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 17
summaryBullets: Now the Philistines gathered their forces for war at Socoh in Judah, and they camped between Socoh and Azekah in Ephes-dammim. (17:1).
Saul and the men of Israel assembled and camped in the Valley of Elah, arraying themselves for battle against the Philistines. (17:2).
The Philistines stood on one hill and the Israelites stood on another, with the valley between them. (17:3).
Then a champion named Goliath, who was from Gath, came out from the Philistine camp. He was six cubits and a span in height, (17:4).
and he had a bronze helmet on his head. He wore a bronze coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, (17:5).
and he had armor of bronze on his legs and a javelin of bronze slung between his shoulders. (17:6).
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and its iron point weighed six hundred shekels. In addition, his shield bearer went before him. (17:7).

And Goliath stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, “Why do you come out and array yourselves for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose one of your men and have him come down against me. (17:8).
If he is able to fight me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and work for us.” (17:9).
Then the Philistine said, “I defy the ranks of Israel this day! Give me a man to fight!” (17:10).
On hearing the words of the Philistine, Saul and all the Israelites were dismayed and greatly afraid. (17:11).
Now David was the son of a man named Jesse, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem of Judah who had eight sons. And in the days of Saul, Jesse was old and well along in years. (17:12).
The three older sons of Jesse had followed Saul into battle: The firstborn was Eliab, the second was Abinadab, and the third was Shammah. (17:13).
And David was the youngest. The three oldest had followed Saul, (17:14).
but David went back and forth from Saul to tend his father’s sheep in Bethlehem. (17:15).
For forty days the Philistine came forward every morning and evening to take his stand. (17:16).
One day Jesse said to his son David, “Take this ephah of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread for your brothers and hurry to their camp. (17:17).
Take also these ten portions of cheese to the commander of their unit. Check on the welfare of your brothers and bring back an assurance from them. (17:18).
They are with Saul and all the men of Israel in the Valley of Elah, fighting against the Philistines.” (17:19).

So David got up early in the morning, left the flock with a keeper, loaded up, and set out as Jesse had instructed him. He reached the camp as the army was marching out to its position and shouting the battle cry. (17:20).
And Israel and the Philistines arrayed in formation against each other. (17:21).
Then David left his supplies in the care of the quartermaster and ran to the battle line. When he arrived, he asked his brothers how they were doing. (17:22).

And as he was speaking with them, suddenly the champion named Goliath, the Philistine from Gath, came forward from the ranks of the Philistines and shouted his usual words, which David also heard. (17:23).
When all the men of Israel saw Goliath, they fled from him in great fear. (17:24).

Now the men of Israel had been saying, “Do you see how this man keeps coming out to defy Israel? To the man who kills him the king will give great riches. And he will give him his daughter in marriage and exempt his father’s house from taxation in Israel.” (17:25).

David asked the men who were standing with him, “What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and removes this disgrace from Israel? Just who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?” (17:26).
The people told him about the offer, saying, “That is what will be done for the man who kills him.” (17:27).

Now when David’s oldest brother Eliab heard him speaking to the men, his anger burned against David. “Why have you come down here?” he asked. “And with whom did you leave those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and wickedness of heart — you have come down to see the battle!” (17:28).
“What have I done now?” said David. “Was it not just a question?” (17:29).
Then he turned from him toward another and asked about the offer, and those people answered him just as the first ones had answered. (17:30).
Now David’s words were overheard and reported to Saul, who sent for him. (17:31).
And David said to Saul, “Let no man’s heart fail on account of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him!” (17:32).
But Saul replied, “You cannot go out against this Philistine to fight him. You are just a boy, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” (17:33).
David replied, “Your servant has been tending his father’s sheep, and whenever a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock, (17:34).
I went after it, struck it down, and delivered the lamb from its mouth. If it reared up against me, I would grab it by its fur, strike it down, and kill it. (17:35).
Your servant has killed lions and bears; this uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God.” (17:36).
David added, “The LORD, who delivered me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine.” “Go,” said Saul, “and may the LORD be with you.” (17:37).
Then Saul clothed David in his own tunic, put a bronze helmet on his head, and dressed him in armor. (17:38).

David strapped his sword over the tunic and tried to walk, but he was not accustomed to them. “I cannot walk in these,” David said to Saul. “I am not accustomed to them.” So David took them off. (17:39).
And David took his staff in his hand, selected five smooth stones from the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag. And with his sling in hand, he approached the Philistine. (17:40).
Now the Philistine came closer and closer to David, with his shield-bearer before him. (17:41).
When the Philistine looked and saw David, he despised him because he was just a boy, ruddy and handsome. (17:42).
“Am I a dog,” he said to David, “that you come at me with sticks?” And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. (17:43).
“Come here,” he called to David, “and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and the beasts of the field!” (17:44).

But David said to the Philistine, “You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. (17:45).

This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand. This day I will strike you down, cut off your head, and give the carcasses of the Philistine army to the birds of the air and the creatures of the earth. Then the whole world will know that there is a God in Israel. (17:46).
And all those assembled here will know that it is not by sword or spear that the LORD saves; for the battle is the LORD’s, and He will give all of you into our hands.” (17:47).
As the Philistine started forward to attack him, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet him. (17:48).
Then David reached into his bag, took out a stone, and slung it, striking the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground. (17:49).
Thus David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and a stone; without a sword in his hand he struck down the Philistine and killed him. (17:50).

David ran and stood over him. He grabbed the Philistine’s sword and pulled it from its sheath and killed him, and he cut off his head with the sword. When the Philistines saw that their hero was dead, they turned and ran. (17:51).

Then the men of Israel and Judah charged forward with a shout and pursued the Philistines to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron. And the bodies of the Philistines were strewn along the Shaaraim road to Gath and Ekron. (17:52).
When the Israelites returned from their pursuit of the Philistines, they plundered their camps. (17:53).
David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, and he put Goliath’s weapons in his own tent. (17:54).

As Saul had watched David going out to confront the Philistine, he said to Abner the commander of the army, “Abner, whose son is this young man?” “As surely as you live, O king,” Abner replied, “I do not know.” (17:55).
“Find out whose son this young man is!” said the king. (17:56).
So when David returned from killing the Philistine, still holding his head in his hand, Abner took him and brought him before Saul. (17:57).
“Whose son are you, young man?” asked Saul. “I am the son of your servant Jesse of Bethlehem,” David replied. (17:58).
crossRefs: Joshua 11:22: Goliath’s city, Gath, one of the remaining Anakim strongholds.
2 Samuel 21:15-22: Other giants from Gath slain later by David and his men.
Judges 15:14-16: Samson slays Philistines with a jawbone (parallel single-handed victory).
Hebrews 11:32-34: Reference to those who 'through faith… stopped the mouths of lions' (David vs. lion/bear).
Sirach 47:4: 'Did he not slay a giant, and take away reproach from the people?'

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אַמָּה (ammah, cubit ~18 in / 45 cm); טֶפַח (tefaḥ, span ~9 in / 22 cm)
translationNotes.note: Height of Goliath calculated as over 9 feet (~2.9 m). Some manuscripts give ~6'9'' (4 cubits, LXX).
Literally 'man of the space between,' meaning single-combat representative.
Weapon for hurling stones with lethal force; shepherds used it against predators.
Jerusalem at this time still held by Jebusites (2 Samuel 5). The act anticipates David’s later conquest and central role there.
The distance between thumb-tip and little-finger-tip with the fingers spread; half a cubit, about 9 inches (23 cm). The breastpiece of the high priest was a span square (Exodus 28:16).
The standard Old Testament dry measure for grain, about 22 quarts or 5.8 gallons (22 liters). Ruth carries home an ephah of barley after a day's gleaning (Ruth 2:17).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵמֶק הָאֵלָה (Emeq ha-Elah), valley of the terebinth
translationNotes.note: A broad valley running from the Judean hills down toward the Philistine plain, about fifteen miles west of Bethlehem, and one of the few routes an army could use to get up into the hills. Verse 1 places the Philistines on one ridge at Socoh and Israel on the other, with the valley between them, exactly as verse 3 describes. The dry streambed in the bottom is where David picked up his five smooth stones.

Verses 5 to 7 weigh Goliath's equipment: a bronze coat of scale armour of five thousand shekels, about 125 pounds, and an iron spearhead of six hundred shekels, about 15 pounds. Iron was the newer and better metal, and the Philistines had it while Israel did not (1 Samuel 13:19-22). The armour bearer walking in front with the shield in verse 7 was standard for a heavy infantry champion.

stories.keyTakeaway: David kills Goliath with a sling, cutting off his head and routing the Philistines. He is introduced to Saul as Jesse’s son.

stories.title: 🤝 1 Samuel 18
summaryBullets: After David had finished speaking with Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan loved him as himself. (18:1).
And from that day Saul kept David with him and did not let him return to his father’s house. (18:2).
Then Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself. (18:3).
And Jonathan removed the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt. (18:4).

So David marched out and prospered in everything Saul sent him to do, and Saul set him over the men of war. And this was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul’s officers as well. (18:5).

As the troops were returning home after David had killed the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing, with joyful songs, and with tambourines and other instruments. (18:6).
And as the women danced, they sang out: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” (18:7).
And Saul was furious and resented this song. “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David,” he said, “but only thousands to me. What more can he have but the kingdom?” (18:8).
And from that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David. (18:9).
The next day a spirit of distress sent from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied inside the house while David played the harp as usual. Now Saul was holding a spear, (18:10).
and he hurled it, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David eluded him twice. (18:11).
So Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. (18:12).
Therefore Saul sent David away and gave him command of a thousand men. David led the troops out to battle and back, (18:13).
and he continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him. (18:14).
When Saul saw that David was very successful, he was afraid of him. (18:15).
But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he was leading them out to battle and back. (18:16).

Then Saul said to David, “Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you in marriage. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD’s battles.” But Saul was thinking, “I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” (18:17).
And David said to Saul, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” (18:18).
So when it was time to give Saul’s daughter Merab to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah. (18:19).
Now Saul’s daughter Michal loved David, and when this was reported to Saul, it pleased him. (18:20).

“I will give her to David,” Saul thought, “so that she may be a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” So Saul said to David, “For a second time now you can be my son-in-law.” (18:21).
Then Saul ordered his servants, “Speak to David privately and tell him, ‘Behold, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore, become his son-in-law.’” (18:22).
But when Saul’s servants relayed these words to David, he replied, “Does it seem trivial in your sight to be the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.” (18:23).
And the servants told Saul what David had said. (18:24).

Saul replied, “Say to David, ‘The king desires no other dowry but a hundred Philistine foreskins as revenge on his enemies.’” But Saul intended to cause David’s death at the hands of the Philistines. (18:25).
When the servants reported these terms to David, he was pleased to become the king’s son-in-law. Before the wedding day arrived, (18:26).

David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought their foreskins and presented them as payment in full to become the king’s son-in-law. Then Saul gave his daughter Michal to David in marriage. (18:27).
When Saul realized that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved David, (18:28).
he grew even more afraid of David. So from then on Saul was David’s enemy. (18:29).
Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul’s officers, so that his name was highly esteemed. (18:30).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 20:14-17: Jonathan asks David for covenant kindness to his house forever and makes him swear to it again.
2 Samuel 9:1-7: David seeks out Mephibosheth for Jonathan's sake and restores all of Saul's land to him.
Genesis 34:11-12: Shechem offers any bride price and gift her family names, showing what a mohar was.
Exodus 22:16-17: A man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin must pay the bride price for her, whether or not her father gives her to him.
1 Samuel 16:14: The Spirit of the LORD departs from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD torments him.

translationNotes.note: A berit is a binding agreement sworn in public, with obligations on both sides and a penalty behind it, and Hebrew does not make one, it cuts one, from the practice of cutting animals in half and passing between the pieces (Genesis 15:9-18). Verse 3 has Jonathan cut one with David, and the covenant is renewed twice more (20:16, 23:18). Its terms are spelled out at 20:14-15, and they run past both their lifetimes: David is not to cut off Jonathan's household when he comes to power, which is the obligation he honours in 2 Samuel 9.

Verse 4 has Jonathan strip off the robe he was wearing and hand it over with his tunic, sword, bow and belt. Clothing and weapons stood for the man who wore them, and handing them across was how an agreement was made visible; that is why cutting the hem off Saul's robe is such a serious act at 24:4-5, and why Samuel reads a torn robe as a kingdom torn away at 15:27-28. What Jonathan gives away is the outfit of the king's son and heir, in front of witnesses.

Verses 6 and 7 describe a fixed custom: women coming out of the towns to meet a returning army with drums, dancing and a sung refrain. Miriam does it at the sea (Exodus 15:20-21) and Jephthah's daughter does it at Mizpah (Judges 11:34). The couplet in verse 7 is built the ordinary way for Hebrew verse, with the second line raising the number of the first, so thousands and tens of thousands is how the form works. Verse 8 has Saul refuse to hear it that way.

A marriage was arranged between households, and the groom paid the bride's father a mohar in silver, livestock, or service; Jacob worked seven years twice over for it (Genesis 29:18-27). Saul names a price of a hundred Philistines in verse 25 precisely because David is poor and the errand should kill him. David brings back two hundred.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jonathan swears a covenant with David and gives him his robes and weapons; David's military success makes Saul jealous and fearful, so Saul tries to kill him with a spear, then manipulates him into marrying his daughter Michal by setting an impossible bride-price of Philistine foreskins, which David fulfills.

stories.title: 🤝 1 Samuel 19
summaryBullets: Then Saul ordered his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Jonathan delighted greatly in David, (19:1).
so he warned David, saying, “My father Saul intends to kill you. Be on your guard in the morning; find a secret place and hide there. (19:2).
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, so I can ask about you. And if I find out anything, I will tell you.” (19:3).

Then Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul and said to him, “The king should not sin against his servant David; he has not sinned against you. In fact, his actions have been highly beneficial to you. (19:4).

He took his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced, so why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David for no reason?” (19:5).
Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan and swore an oath: “As surely as the LORD lives, David will not be put to death.” (19:6).
So Jonathan summoned David and told him all these things. Then Jonathan brought David to Saul, and David was with Saul as before. (19:7).
When war broke out again, David went out and fought the Philistines and struck them with such a mighty blow that they fled before him. (19:8).
But as Saul was sitting in his house with his spear in his hand, a spirit of distress from the LORD came upon him. While David was playing the harp, (19:9).
Saul tried to pin him to the wall with his spear. But David eluded him and the spear struck the wall. And David fled and escaped that night. (19:10).
Then Saul sent messengers to David’s house to watch him and kill him in the morning. But David’s wife Michal warned him, “If you do not run for your life tonight, tomorrow you will be dead!” (19:11).
So Michal lowered David from the window, and he ran away and escaped. (19:12).
Then Michal took a household idol and laid it in the bed, placed some goat hair on its head, and covered it with a garment. (19:13).
When Saul sent the messengers to seize David, Michal said, “He is ill.” (19:14).
But Saul sent the messengers back to see David and told them, “Bring him up to me in his bed so I can kill him.” (19:15).
And when the messengers entered, there was the idol in the bed with the goat hair on its head. (19:16).
And Saul said to Michal, “Why did you deceive me like this? You sent my enemy away, and he has escaped!” Michal replied, “He said to me, ‘Help me get away, or I will kill you!’” (19:17).
So David ran away and escaped. And he went to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went to Naioth and stayed there. (19:18).
When Saul was told that David was at Naioth in Ramah, (19:19).

he sent messengers to seize him. But when they saw the group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel leading them, the Spirit of God came upon them, and Saul’s messengers also began to prophesy. (19:20).
When this was reported to Saul, he sent more messengers, but they began to prophesy as well. So Saul tried again and sent messengers a third time, and even they began to prophesy. (19:21).
Finally, Saul himself left for Ramah and came to the large cistern at Secu, where he asked, “Where are Samuel and David?” “At Naioth in Ramah,” he was told. (19:22).
So Saul went to Naioth in Ramah. But the Spirit of God came upon even Saul, and he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah. (19:23).
Then Saul stripped off his robes and also prophesied before Samuel. And he collapsed and lay naked all that day and night. That is why it is said, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (19:24).
crossRefs: Genesis 31:19,30-35: Rachel steals her father's household gods and hides them under the camel's saddle to sit on.
Judges 17:5: Micah makes an ephod and household gods and installs one of his own sons as his priest.
Joshua 2:15: Rahab lets the spies down by a rope through the window, because her house was built into the city wall.
1 Samuel 10:9-12: Saul prophesies among the prophets, and the saying begins, is Saul also among the prophets.
Psalm 59:1-4: A psalm of David headed as from the night Saul sent men to watch the house in order to kill him.

translationNotes.note: Teraphim are images kept in a private house rather than at a sanctuary. Rachel steals her father's and hides them in a camel saddle (Genesis 31:19, 34), Micah has a set made for his own shrine (Judges 17:5), Ezekiel 21:21 shows a king consulting them for omens, and Josiah sweeps them out of Judah with the mediums and the idols (2 Kings 23:24). Verse 13 has Michal lay one in the bed with goat hair at its head and a garment over it, and it passes for a sleeping man, so at least some of them were man-sized.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּם נָקִי (dam naqi), innocent blood
translationNotes.note: Jonathan's argument in verses 4 and 5 is a legal one, and he makes it in the technical vocabulary. He states David's service, then puts the charge: why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause. Shedding innocent blood is named as its own offence in Deuteronomy 19:10 and 27:25, and it defiles the land itself (Numbers 35:33). Saul answers it correctly in verse 6, with an oath, and breaks the oath four verses later.

Verse 12 works because of how towns were built. Houses were set against or into the town wall, so a window on the outer side opened onto the drop outside the defences, which is how Rahab lowers the two spies out of Jericho (Joshua 2:15) and how the disciples at Damascus let Paul down in a basket (Acts 9:25). Michal gets David past the men watching the door of the house by putting him outside the town altogether.

translationNotes.term: Is Saul also among the prophets
translationNotes.note: The book records the same saying twice, at 10:11 and again in verse 24, and each time notes that it became a proverb. In the first case Saul prophesies on the day he is anointed; in the second the Spirit falls on three sets of his own assassins and then on him, and he strips off his robes and lies on the ground a day and a night while David gets clear. The writer gives the saying without deciding for the reader whether it is said in wonder or in mockery.

stories.keyTakeaway: Saul orders David's death, but Jonathan convinces him to spare David; when Saul's murderous intent returns, David escapes with help from his wife Michal and finds refuge with Samuel, while Saul's attempts to capture David at Ramah are thwarted as God's Spirit causes his men and finally Saul himself to prophesy.

stories.title: 🤝 1 Samuel 20
summaryBullets: Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah. He came to Jonathan and asked, “What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?” (20:1).
“Far from it!” Jonathan replied. “You will not die. Indeed, my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. So why would he hide this matter from me? This cannot be true!” (20:2).

But David again vowed, “Your father knows very well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he has said, ‘Jonathan must not know of this, or he will be grieved.’ As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, there is but a step between me and death.” (20:3).
Then Jonathan said to David, “Whatever you desire, I will do for you.” (20:4).
So David told him, “Look, tomorrow is the New Moon, and I am supposed to dine with the king. Instead, let me go and hide in the field until the third evening from now. (20:5).
If your father misses me at all, tell him, ‘David urgently requested my permission to hurry to Bethlehem, his hometown, because there is an annual sacrifice for his whole clan.’ (20:6).
If he says, ‘Good,’ then your servant is safe, but if he is enraged, you will know he has evil intentions. (20:7).

Therefore show kindness to your servant, for you have brought me into a covenant with you before the LORD. If there is iniquity in me, then kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?” (20:8).
“Never!” Jonathan replied. “If I ever found out that my father had evil intentions against you, would I not tell you?” (20:9).
Then David asked Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?” (20:10).
“Come,” he replied, “let us go out to the field.” So the two of them went out into the field, (20:11).
and Jonathan said, “By the LORD, the God of Israel, I will sound out my father by this time tomorrow or the next day. If he is favorable toward you, will I not send for you and tell you? (20:12).

But if my father intends to bring evil on you, then may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if I do not tell you and send you on your way in safety. May the LORD be with you, just as He has been with my father. (20:13).
And as long as I live, treat me with the LORD’s loving devotion, that I may not die, (20:14).
and do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household— not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth.” (20:15).
So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, “May the LORD hold David’s enemies accountable.” (20:16).
And Jonathan had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself. (20:17).
Then Jonathan said to David, “Tomorrow is the New Moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty. (20:18).
When you have stayed three days, hurry down to the place you hid on the day this trouble began, and remain beside the stone Ezel. (20:19).
I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as if I were aiming at a target. (20:20).

Then I will send a boy and say, ‘Go, find the arrows!’ Now, if I expressly say to him, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you; bring them,’ then come, because as surely as the LORD lives, it is safe for you, and there is no danger. (20:21).
But if I say to the young man, ‘Look, the arrows are beyond you,’ then you must go, for the LORD has sent you away. (20:22).
And as for the matter you and I have discussed, the LORD is a witness between you and me forever.” (20:23).
So David hid in the field, and when the New Moon had come, the king sat down to eat. (20:24).
He sat in his usual place by the wall, opposite Jonathan and beside Abner, but David’s place was empty. (20:25).
Saul said nothing that day because he thought, “Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean— surely he is unclean.” (20:26).
But on the day after the New Moon, the second day, David’s place was still empty, and Saul asked his son Jonathan, “Why hasn’t the son of Jesse come to the meal either yesterday or today?” (20:27).
Jonathan answered, “David urgently requested my permission to go to Bethlehem, (20:28).

saying, ‘Please let me go, because our clan is holding a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has told me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.” (20:29).

Then Saul’s anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame and to the shame of the mother who bore you? (20:30).
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Now send for him and bring him to me, for he must surely die!” (20:31).
“Why must he be put to death?” Jonathan replied. “What has he done?” (20:32).
Then Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David. (20:33).
Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger and did not eat any food that second day of the month, for he was grieved by his father’s shameful treatment of David. (20:34).
In the morning Jonathan went out to the field for the appointment with David, and a small boy was with him. (20:35).
He said to the boy, “Run and find the arrows I shoot.” And as the boy ran, Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him. (20:36).
When the boy reached the place where Jonathan’s arrow had fallen, Jonathan called to him, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?” (20:37).
Then Jonathan cried out, “Hurry! Make haste! Do not delay!” So the boy picked up the arrow and returned to his master. (20:38).
But the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the arrangement. (20:39).
Then Jonathan gave his equipment to the boy and said, “Go, take it back to the city.” (20:40).

When the young man had gone, David got up from the south side of the stone, fell facedown, and bowed three times. Then he and Jonathan kissed each other and wept together — though David wept more. (20:41).

And Jonathan said to David, “Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD, saying, ‘May the LORD be a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever.’” Then David got up and departed, and Jonathan went back into the city. (20:42).
crossRefs: Numbers 10:10: On your appointed feasts and at the beginnings of your months you shall blow the trumpets over your offerings.
Numbers 28:11-15: The burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings appointed for the first day of every month.
Leviticus 7:19-21: Anyone who is unclean and eats the flesh of the peace offering is cut off from his people.
2 Samuel 21:7: David spares Mephibosheth because of the oath of the LORD sworn between him and Jonathan.
1 Samuel 23:16-18: Jonathan finds David at Horesh, strengthens his hand in God, and the two make a covenant again.

translationNotes.note: Chesed is loyalty that a person owes because of a relationship they have entered, and holds to when they no longer have to. It is not affection and it is not charity; the nearest English is faithfulness under obligation. Verse 8 has David appeal to it as a claim under the covenant, and verses 14 and 15 have Jonathan ask for it in return, for himself and then for his household after him, which is the clause David honours when he sends for Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel 9.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִשְׁפָּחָה (mishpachah), clan or extended family
translationNotes.note: The excuse in verses 6 and 29 has to be believable, and it is because the mishpachah, the whole extended family, held its own annual sacrifice, and every man of it was expected there. Israelite society ran in three layers, the tribe, the clan and the father's house, and the clan is the layer that owned land in common, avenged blood and redeemed a poor relative's property. Being absent from its sacrifice was a public matter, which is exactly why the excuse is worth telling and why Saul's reaction in verse 30 is aimed at David's family line.

Verses 20 to 22 and 35 to 40 set up a signal that carries in the open. Jonathan cannot risk being seen with David, so the message is coded into what he shouts at a boy fetching arrows, and the boy has no idea he is carrying it. Then Jonathan hands the boy his weapons and sends him back to town, which clears the field so the two men can speak. It is careful work by a man whose father has already thrown a spear at him that day.

Israel's months began with the sighting of the new crescent, and the first of the month was marked by trumpet blasts and set offerings (Numbers 10:10, 28:11-15). At court it meant a feast with assigned seats, which is why an empty place could not be missed. David expects to be missed on the first day and is only questioned on the second (verses 25 to 27).

stories.keyTakeaway: David asks Jonathan to test whether Saul intends to kill him; Jonathan swears a covenant oath to warn David by shooting arrows, and after Saul's rage at the feast confirms his murderous intent, Jonathan signals David to flee.

headings.text: Jonathan and David Renew Their Covenant

stories.title: 🏹 1 Samuel 21
summaryBullets: Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And when Ahimelech met David, he trembled and asked him, “Why are you alone? Why is no one with you?” (21:1).
“The king has given me a mission,” David replied. “He told me no one is to know about the mission on which I am sending you. And I have directed my young men to meet me at a certain place. (21:2).
Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever can be found.” (21:3).
“There is no common bread on hand,” the priest replied, “but there is some consecrated bread — provided that the young men have kept themselves from women.” (21:4).
David answered, “Women have indeed been kept from us, as is usual when I set out. And the bodies of the young men are holy even on common missions. How much more so today!” (21:5).

So the priest gave him the consecrated bread, since there was no bread there but the Bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD and replaced with hot bread on the day it was taken away. (21:6).
Now one of Saul’s servants was there that day, detained before the LORD. And his name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief shepherd for Saul. (21:7).
Then David asked Ahimelech, “Is there not a spear or sword on hand here? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king’s mission was urgent.” (21:8).

The priest replied, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here; it is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want, you may take it. For there is no other but this one here.” And David said, “There is none like it; give it to me.” (21:9).
That day David fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath. (21:10).

But the servants of Achish said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing about him in their dances, saying: ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?” (21:11).
Now David took these words to heart and was very much afraid of Achish the king of Gath. (21:12).
So he changed his behavior before them and feigned madness in their hands; he scratched on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard. (21:13).
Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me? (21:14).
Am I in need of madmen, that you have brought this man to rave in my presence? Must this man come into my house?” (21:15).
crossRefs: Leviticus 24:5-9: Twelve loaves are set out before the LORD every sabbath, and Aaron and his sons eat them in a holy place.
Matthew 12:1-8: Jesus cites David eating the bread of the Presence when His disciples are accused of breaking the sabbath.
Mark 2:23-28: The same account, closing with the sabbath made for man and not man for the sabbath.
1 Samuel 17:50-51: David kills Goliath with a sling and cuts off his head with the giant's own sword.
Psalm 34:1-8: A psalm of David headed as from the time he changed his behaviour before Abimelech, who drove him out.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים (lechem ha-panim), bread of the face
translationNotes.note: Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, were set out in two rows on a gold table in the holy place every sabbath, with frankincense beside them, and the loaves taken off were to be eaten by the priests in a holy place, and by nobody else (Leviticus 24:5-9, Exodus 25:30). Verses 4 to 6 have Ahimelech hand the week's bread to a layman and his men because there is no common bread in the sanctuary. Jesus cites this incident by name when He is challenged about His disciples picking grain on the sabbath (Matthew 12:3-4).

Verse 9 keeps the sword wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at the sanctuary. Captured weapons were dedicated as trophies and stored there, which is why the priest knows exactly where it is; 2 Kings 11:10 has the spears and shields that had been King David's still kept in the house of the LORD and handed out to the guard at Joash's coronation. The man collecting it is the man who took it, and he is on his way to Gath, the dead owner's home town.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶעְצָר לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (netsar lifne YHWH), detained before the LORD
translationNotes.note: Verse 7 stops to record who else was at Nob that day. Doeg is an Edomite, from Israel's oldest rival nation, and he holds a senior royal post as Saul's chief herdsman, which in that world meant charge of the crown's livestock and the men who worked it. The odd phrase detained before the LORD says he was being held at the sanctuary, under some obligation the text does not name. He is the only witness, and chapter 22 is what he does with it.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיְשַׁנּוֹ אֶת־טַעְמוֹ (vayeshanno et-taamo), he changed his behaviour
translationNotes.note: Verses 12 to 15 have David scratch at the doors of the gate and let spittle run into his beard in front of the king of Gath. Madness was widely treated as something touched by a god, so a madman was left alone rather than killed, and Achish says as much: do I lack madmen, that you bring me this one. The beard mattered too, since a man's beard was his dignity, and fouling it was the plainest way to look like a man who had lost his mind.

After Shiloh was destroyed the sanctuary and the priestly families settled at Nob, on the ridge just north of Jerusalem within sight of the city; 1 Samuel 22:19 calls it the city of the priests. The ephod, the bread of the Presence, and Goliath's sword are all kept there. Saul wipes the town out in chapter 22, and it never appears again as a sanctuary.

stories.keyTakeaway: David obtains consecrated bread and Goliath's sword from Ahimelek at Nob, then flees to Achish king of Gath; when recognized as a threat, David feigns madness to escape.

stories.title: 🏹 1 Samuel 22
summaryBullets: So David left Gath and took refuge in the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and the rest of his father’s household heard about it, they went down to him there. (22:1).
And all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him, and he became their leader. About four hundred men were with him. (22:2).
From there David went to Mizpeh of Moab, where he said to the king of Moab, “Please let my father and mother stay with you until I learn what God will do for me.” (22:3).
So he left them in the care of the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time David was in the stronghold. (22:4).
Then the prophet Gad said to David, “Do not stay in the stronghold. Depart and go into the land of Judah.” So David left and went to the forest of Hereth. (22:5).

Soon Saul learned that David and his men had been discovered. At that time Saul was sitting under the tamarisk tree on the hill at Gibeah, with his spear in hand and all his servants standing around him. (22:6).
Then Saul said to his servants, “Listen, men of Benjamin! Is the son of Jesse giving all of you fields and vineyards and making you commanders of thousands or hundreds? (22:7).

Is that why all of you have conspired against me? Not one of you told me that my own son had made a covenant with the son of Jesse. Not one of you has shown concern for me or revealed to me that my son has stirred up my own servant to lie in wait against me, as is the case today.” (22:8).
But Doeg the Edomite, who had stationed himself with Saul’s servants, answered: “I saw the son of Jesse come to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob. (22:9).
Ahimelech inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions. He also gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine.” (22:10).
Then the king sent messengers to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and his father’s whole family, who were priests at Nob. And all of them came to the king. (22:11).
“Listen now, son of Ahitub,” said Saul. “Here I am, my lord,” he replied. (22:12).

And Saul asked him, “Why have you and the son of Jesse conspired against me? You gave him bread and a sword and inquired of God for him so that he could rise up against me to lie in wait, as he is doing today.” (22:13).
Ahimelech answered the king, “Who among all your servants is as faithful as David, the king’s son-in-law, the captain of your bodyguard and honored in your house? (22:14).

Was that day the first time I inquired of God for him? Far be it from me! Let not the king accuse your servant or any of my father’s household, for your servant knew nothing of this whole affair — not in part or in whole.” (22:15).
But the king replied, “You will surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father’s house!” (22:16).

Then the king ordered the guards at his side, “Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because they too sided with David. For they knew he was fleeing, but they did not tell me.” But the king’s servants would not lift a hand to strike the priests of the LORD. (22:17).

So the king ordered Doeg, “You turn and strike down the priests!” And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests himself. On that day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. (22:18).
He also put to the sword Nob, the city of the priests, with its men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep. (22:19).
But one of the sons of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped. His name was Abiathar, and he fled to David. (22:20).
And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD. (22:21).
Then David said to Abiathar, “I knew that Doeg the Edomite was there that day, and that he was sure to tell Saul. I myself am responsible for the lives of everyone in your father’s house. (22:22).
Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks your life is seeking mine as well. You will be safe with me.” (22:23).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 2:31-33: The word that God would cut off the strength of Eli's house, so that no old man would be left in it.
1 Kings 2:26-27: Solomon removes Abiathar from the priesthood, fulfilling the word spoken against Eli's house at Shiloh.
Psalm 52:1-9: A psalm of David headed as from when Doeg the Edomite told Saul that David had come to Ahimelech's house.
Psalm 142:1-7: A prayer of David headed as from the cave, when no one would look on his right hand or care for his soul.
Ruth 4:17-22: David's line traced through Obed and Boaz to Ruth the Moabitess, whose people shelter his parents here.

translationNotes.note: Verse 6 has Saul holding court in the open on the hill at Gibeah, sitting under a tamarisk tree with his spear in his hand and his servants standing round him. The spear is Saul's mark of office throughout the book, the way a sceptre is elsewhere: it is in his hand when he throws it at David (18:10-11, 19:9-10), it is stuck in the ground by his head when he sleeps (26:7), and it is what David's men take as proof they were there. There is no throne room; the king sits under a tree.

Saul's question in verse 7 assumes a system his hearers know. A king rewarded his officers with grants of land out of the crown estate and out of property that fell in, which is precisely what Samuel had warned about at 8:14, that he will take the best of your fields and vineyards and give them to his servants. Saul is asking his Benjaminite officers what a Judahite claimant could possibly offer them that he cannot.

The men Saul orders to kill the priests in verse 17 are the ratsim, the royal guard who ran beside the king and stood at the palace door; 1 Kings 14:27-28 has them carrying the bronze shields in and out of the guardroom. They are soldiers under direct royal command with no right of refusal, and they refuse anyway, and the text says why: they would not put out their hand against the priests of the LORD. Saul has to turn to a foreigner to get it done.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְפִי־חֶרֶב (lefi cherev), to the edge of the sword
translationNotes.note: Verses 18 and 19 report eighty-five priests killed in one day, and then the town itself, men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys and sheep. That formula is the vocabulary of the ban, which Saul had refused to carry out against Amalek in chapter 15; here he applies it in full to an Israelite town of priests. One son of Ahimelech gets out, Abiathar, who reaches David with the ephod, and Solomon's removal of him years later is recorded as the end of the line of Eli (1 Kings 2:26-27).

Adullam sits in the low chalk hills between the Judean highlands and the Philistine plain, about ten miles southwest of Bethlehem, in country riddled with caves. It was borderland, close enough to raid from and awkward for either side to hold. The four hundred men who gather to David in verse 2 are described as in distress, in debt, and bitter in soul, which is who ends up in that country.

stories.keyTakeaway: David gathers four hundred distressed men at Adullam, leaves his parents with the king of Moab, and moves to the forest of Hereth; Saul learns David visited the priest Ahimelek at Nob and orders the massacre of the priests there, though Ahimelek's son Abiathar escapes to David.

headings.text: David Flees to Adullam and Mizpeh
Saul Slays the Priests of Nob

stories.title: 🏹 1 Samuel 23
summaryBullets: Now it was reported to David, “Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and looting the threshing floors.” (23:1).
So David inquired of the LORD, “Should I go and attack these Philistines?” And the LORD said to David, “Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah.” (23:2).
But David’s men said to him, “Look, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?” (23:3).
Once again, David inquired of the LORD, and the LORD answered him: “Go at once to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.” (23:4).
