Then David and his men went to Keilah, fought against the Philistines, and carried off their livestock, striking them with a mighty blow. So David saved the people of Keilah. (23:5).
(Now Abiathar son of Ahimelech had brought the ephod with him when he fled to David at Keilah.) (23:6).
When Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah, he said, “God has delivered him into my hand, for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars.” (23:7).
Then Saul summoned all his troops to go to war at Keilah and besiege David and his men. (23:8).
When David learned that Saul was plotting evil against him, he said to Abiathar the priest, “Bring the ephod.” (23:9).
And David said, “O LORD, God of Israel, Your servant has heard that Saul intends to come to Keilah and destroy the city on my account. (23:10).
Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as Your servant has heard? O LORD, God of Israel, please tell Your servant.” “He will,” said the LORD. (23:11).
So David asked, “Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?” “They will,” said the LORD. (23:12).

Then David and his men, about six hundred strong, set out and departed from Keilah, moving from place to place. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he declined to go forth. (23:13).
And David stayed in the wilderness strongholds and in the hill country of the Wilderness of Ziph. Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand. (23:14).
While David was in Horesh in the Wilderness of Ziph, he saw that Saul had come out to take his life. (23:15).
And Saul’s son Jonathan came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God, (23:16).
saying, “Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you. And you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command. Even my father Saul knows this is true.” (23:17).
So the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. And David remained in Horesh, while Jonathan went home. (23:18).
Then the Ziphites came up to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon? (23:19).
Now, O king, come down whenever your soul desires, and we will be responsible for delivering him into your hand.” (23:20).
“May you be blessed by the LORD,” replied Saul, “for you have had compassion on me. (23:21).
Please go and prepare further. Investigate and watch carefully where he goes and who has seen him there, for I am told that he is extremely cunning. (23:22).
Observe and find out all the places where he hides. Then come back to me with certainty, and I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the clans of Judah.” (23:23).
So they set out and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the Wilderness of Maon in the Arabah south of Jeshimon, (23:24).
and Saul and his men went to seek him. When David was told about it, he went down to the rock and stayed in the Wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard of this, he pursued David there. (23:25).

Saul was proceeding along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other side. Even though David was hurrying to get away, Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them. (23:26).
Then a messenger came to Saul, saying, “Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!” (23:27).
So Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why that place is called Sela-hammahlekoth. (23:28).
And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En-gedi. (23:29).
crossRefs: Exodus 28:29-30: The Urim and the Thummim are put in the breastpiece of judgment, over Aaron's heart before the LORD.
Numbers 27:21: Joshua shall stand before Eleazar, who will inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD.
1 Samuel 22:20-23: Abiathar escapes the killing at Nob and comes down to David with the ephod in his hand.
Psalm 54:1-7: A psalm of David headed as from when the Ziphites came and told Saul that David was hiding among them.
Joshua 15:44,55: Keilah, Ziph, and Maon listed among the towns given to Judah in the lowland and the hill country.

translationNotes.note: The high priest's ephod was a vestment with the breastpiece fixed to the front of it, and the Urim and Thummim carried in the fold of that breastpiece (Exodus 28:6-30). Because the means of putting a question to God hung on it, bring the ephod came to mean bring me an answer, which is exactly how David uses it in verse 9. Verses 10 to 12 show the method working: he asks two questions, each shaped so that yes or no will do, and gets an answer to each. Abiathar carried it out of Nob when Saul destroyed the town.

Verse 1 has the Philistines looting the threshing floors at Keilah, which dates the raid and explains it. Threshing happens in the weeks after the harvest, when the whole year's grain is lying in the open on flat ground outside the town, unguarded and easy to carry off. Raiding at that moment takes the food and leaves the town to starve, which is what Midian did to Israel in Judges 6:3-6. Keilah is a walled town with gates and bars (verse 7), which is what makes David's position there a trap.

The wilderness of Judah is the eastern side of the Judean ridge, dropping from about three thousand feet above the sea near Hebron to thirteen hundred feet below it at the Dead Sea in the space of some fifteen miles. The hills cut off the rain, so it is bare rock, ravines and caves with a few springs, empty of settlement and impossible to search properly. Ziph, Maon, Carmel and En-gedi are all on that edge. It is why David can live within a few miles of Saul for years.
Place named for David’s narrow escape when Saul was diverted to fight Philistines.

stories.keyTakeaway: David defeats the Philistines at Keilah, but learns the townspeople would betray him to Saul, so he flees to the wilderness; Jonathan visits him to encourage him, the Ziphites inform Saul of his location, and a Philistine raid forces Saul to abandon his pursuit.

stories.title: ⛰️ 1 Samuel 24
summaryBullets: After Saul had returned from pursuing the Philistines, he was told, “David is in the wilderness of En-gedi.” (24:1).
So Saul took three thousand chosen men from all Israel and went to look for David and his men in the region of the Rocks of the Wild Goats. (24:2).
Soon Saul came to the sheepfolds along the road, where there was a cave, and he went in to relieve himself. And David and his men were hiding in the recesses of the cave. (24:3).

So David’s men said to him, “This is the day about which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish.’” Then David crept up and stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe. (24:4).
Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe. (24:5).
So he said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do such a thing to my master, the LORD’s anointed. May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.” (24:6).
With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul. Then Saul left the cave and went on his way. (24:7).
After that, David got up, went out of the cave, and called out to Saul, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed facedown in reverence (24:8).
and said to Saul, “Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ‘Look, David intends to harm you’ ? (24:9).

Behold, this day you have seen with your own eyes that the LORD delivered you into my hand in the cave. I was told to kill you, but I spared you and said, ‘I will not lift my hand against my lord, since he is the LORD’s anointed.’ (24:10).

See, my father, look at the corner of your robe in my hand. For I cut it off, but I did not kill you. Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands. I have not sinned against you, even though you are hunting me down to take my life. (24:11).
May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you. (24:12).
As the old proverb says, ‘Wickedness proceeds from the wicked.’ But my hand will never be against you. (24:13).
Against whom has the king of Israel come out? Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea? (24:14).
May the LORD be our judge and decide between you and me. May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand.” (24:15).
When David had finished saying these things, Saul called back, “Is that your voice, David my son?” Then Saul wept aloud (24:16).
and said to David, “You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil. (24:17).
And you have declared this day how you have treated me well, for when the LORD delivered me into your hand, you did not kill me. (24:18).
When a man finds his enemy, does he let him go away unharmed? May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day. (24:19).
Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands. (24:20).
So now, swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house.” (24:21).
So David gave his oath to Saul. Then Saul returned home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold. (24:22).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 26:7-12: David refuses again to strike Saul, and takes the spear and water jug from beside his head instead.
Exodus 22:28: You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
Deuteronomy 32:35: Vengeance is Mine and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip.
Romans 12:19: Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, vengeance is Mine, I will repay.
Psalm 57:1-11: A psalm of David headed as from when he fled from Saul into the cave, taking refuge in the shadow of God's wings.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְהָסֵךְ אֶת־רַגְלָיו (le-hasekh et-raglav); literally 'to cover his feet'
translationNotes.note: Euphemism for urination/defecation; Saul entered the cave vulnerable.

translationNotes.term: Swear you will not cut off my descendants
translationNotes.note: Saul's request in verse 21 sounds odd until you know what usually happened. A new dynasty in Israel wiped out the old one to the last male, so that no claimant survived: Baasha destroys the whole house of Jeroboam (1 Kings 15:29), Zimri destroys the house of Baasha (1 Kings 16:11), and Jehu has Ahab's seventy sons beheaded (2 Kings 10:1-8). Saul is asking for the exception, and verse 22 has David swear it. He keeps it in 2 Samuel 9.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵין גֶּדִי (Ein Gedi), spring of the kid
translationNotes.note: A freshwater spring and waterfall on the west shore of the Dead Sea, about 1,300 feet below sea level, with dry cliffs rising steeply behind it and caves cut into them by the water. It is the only reliable water for miles, which is why both David and Saul are there. Verse 2 has Saul searching among the Rocks of the Wild Goats, the name for that broken ground.

The hem of an outer robe was where a man's identity and authority sat: it carried tassels commanded in Numbers 15:38-39, and a seal impression in the hem served as a signature on documents. Cutting it off was not a joke about clothing. Verse 5 says David's heart struck him afterward, and 1 Samuel 15:27-28 uses a torn robe hem for the kingdom being torn away.

stories.keyTakeaway: David finds Saul alone in a cave and cuts off a piece of his robe but spares his life; when David reveals this to Saul, Saul weeps, acknowledges David's righteousness, and makes David swear not to destroy his descendants.

stories.title: ⛰️ 1 Samuel 25
summaryBullets: When Samuel died, all Israel gathered to mourn for him; and they buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David set out and went down to the Wilderness of Paran. (25:1).
Now there was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. He was a very wealthy man with a thousand goats and three thousand sheep, which he was shearing in Carmel. (25:2).
His name was Nabal, and his wife’s name was Abigail. She was an intelligent and beautiful woman, but her husband, a Calebite, was harsh and evil in his dealings. (25:3).
While David was in the wilderness, he heard that Nabal was shearing sheep. (25:4).
So David sent ten young men and instructed them, “Go up to Nabal at Carmel. Greet him in my name (25:5).
and say to him, ‘Long life to you, and peace to you and to your house and to all that belongs to you. (25:6).
Now I hear that it is time for shearing. When your shepherds were with us, we did not harass them, and nothing of theirs was missing the whole time they were in Carmel. (25:7).

Ask your young men, and they will tell you. So let my young men find favor with you, for we have come on the day of a feast. Please give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.’” (25:8).
When David’s young men arrived, they relayed all these words to Nabal on behalf of David. Then they waited. (25:9).
But Nabal asked them, “Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse? Many servants these days are breaking away from their masters. (25:10).
Why should I take my bread and water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, and give them to these men whose origin I do not know?” (25:11).
So David’s men turned around and went back, and they relayed to him all these words. (25:12).
And David said to his men, “Strap on your swords!” So David and all his men strapped on their swords, and about four hundred men followed David, while two hundred stayed with the supplies. (25:13).
Meanwhile, one of Nabal’s young men informed Nabal’s wife Abigail, “Look, David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he screamed at them. (25:14).
Yet these men were very good to us. When we were in the field, we were not harassed, and nothing of ours went missing the whole time we lived among them. (25:15).
They were a wall around us, both day and night, the whole time we were herding our sheep near them. (25:16).
Now consider carefully what you must do, because disaster looms over our master and all his household. For he is such a scoundrel that nobody can speak to him!” (25:17).

Then Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five butchered sheep, five seahs of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs. She loaded them on donkeys (25:18).
and said to her young men, “Go ahead of me. I will be right behind you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal. (25:19).
As Abigail came riding her donkey into a mountain ravine, she saw David and his men coming down toward her, and she met them. (25:20).
Now David had just said, “In vain I have protected all that belonged to this man in the wilderness. Nothing that belongs to him has gone missing, yet he has paid me back evil for good. (25:21).
May God punish David, and ever so severely, if I let one male belonging to Nabal survive until morning.” (25:22).
When Abigail saw David, she quickly got off the donkey, fell facedown, and bowed before him. (25:23).
She fell at his feet and said, “My lord, may the blame be on me alone, but please let your servant speak to you; hear the words of your servant. (25:24).

My lord should pay no attention to this scoundrel Nabal, for he lives up to his name: His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him. I, your servant, did not see my lord’s young men whom you sent. (25:25).

Now, my lord, as surely as the LORD lives and you yourself live, since the LORD has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand, may your enemies and those who seek harm for my lord be like Nabal. (25:26).
Now let this gift your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow you. (25:27).
Please forgive your servant’s offense, for the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles. May no evil be found in you as long as you live. (25:28).

And should someone pursue you and seek your life, then the life of my lord will be bound securely by the LORD your God in the bundle of the living. But He shall fling away the lives of your enemies like stones from a sling. (25:29).
When the LORD has done for my lord all the good He promised, and when He has appointed you ruler over Israel, (25:30).
then my lord will have no remorse or guilt of conscience over needless bloodshed and revenge. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, may you remember your servant.” (25:31).
Then David said to Abigail, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day! (25:32).
Blessed is your discernment, and blessed are you, because today you kept me from bloodshed and from avenging myself by my own hand. (25:33).

Otherwise, as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has restrained me from harming you, if you had not come quickly to meet me, then surely no male belonging to Nabal would have been left alive by morning light.” (25:34).
Then David accepted from her hand what she had brought him, and he said to her, “Go home in peace. See, I have heeded your voice and granted your request.” (25:35).
When Abigail returned to Nabal, there he was in the house, holding a feast fit for a king, in high spirits and very drunk. So she told him nothing until morning light. (25:36).
In the morning when Nabal was sober, his wife told him about these events, and his heart failed within him, and he became like a stone. (25:37).
About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal dead. (25:38).

On hearing that Nabal was dead, David said, “Blessed be the LORD, who has upheld my cause against the reproach of Nabal and has restrained His servant from evil. For the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” Then David sent word to Abigail, asking her to become his wife. (25:39).
When his servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they said, “David has sent us to take you as his wife.” (25:40).
She arose, bowed facedown, and said, “Here is your servant, ready to serve and to wash the feet of my lord’s servants.” (25:41).
So Abigail hurried and got on a donkey, and attended by five of her maidens, she followed David’s messengers and became his wife. (25:42).
David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. So she and Abigail were both his wives. (25:43).
But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim. (25:44).
crossRefs: Genesis 38:12-13: Judah goes up to his sheepshearers at Timnah, the seasonal feast of a man with large flocks.
2 Samuel 13:23-29: Absalom holds a sheepshearing feast at Baal-hazor and has Amnon killed there.
Deuteronomy 32:35: Vengeance is Mine and recompense, for the time when their foot shall slip.
Proverbs 15:1: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
Joshua 14:13-15: Hebron is given to Caleb son of Jephunneh for an inheritance, the family Nabal belonged to.

translationNotes.note: Hebrew uses the plural of blood for blood that has been shed unlawfully and for the liability it creates. It is not a feeling of guilt; it is a debt that attaches to the killer and to his house until it is settled, and Numbers 35:33 says such blood pollutes the land and nothing cleanses it but the blood of the man who shed it. That is what Abigail heads off in verses 26 to 31 and what David thanks God for in verse 33: he had set out to kill a household over an insult, which would have put blood on his own name before he was ever king.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: כַּרְמֶל (Karmel), orchard or garden land
translationNotes.note: Verse 2 puts Nabal's business at Carmel, and this is not Mount Carmel by the sea where Elijah faced the prophets of Baal. It is a town in the hills of Judah about seven miles south of Hebron, near Maon, on the edge of the wilderness where the grazing runs out. Saul had set up a monument for himself there after the Amalekite campaign (15:12). The word simply means garden land, so more than one place carries it.

David's oath in verses 22 and 34 is coarse in the original and every English version tidies it. The Hebrew says he will not leave alive one who urinates against a wall, which is a blunt way of saying every male in the household. It is a fixed idiom of threat, used four more times, all of them about wiping out a man's line: 1 Kings 14:10, 16:11 and 21:21, and 2 Kings 9:8. The vulgarity is part of the temper the chapter is describing.

About 7 quarts (7 liters); one third of an ephah. The 'three measures of flour' in the parable of the leaven (Matthew 13:33) are three seahs / roughly 30-40 lbs of flour, enough to feed a sizeable household for days.

Shearing came at the end of spring and was the one day a year a flock owner turned his wool into money. It was kept as a feast with hired hands, food, and wine, and neighbours expected a share. David's request in verses 7 and 8 is made at that season on the strength of having guarded Nabal's shepherds all winter, which is why the refusal is an insult and not just a no.

His wife says it outright in verse 25: his name is Fool, and folly is with him. The Hebrew naval is not a word for a simpleton but for a man who is morally worthless and treats obligations with contempt, the same word Psalm 14:1 uses of the man who says there is no God. The chapter is built around a man whose name is a verdict.

stories.keyTakeaway: Samuel dies and is buried; David later encounters the wealthy but churlish Nabal, who refuses his request for provisions. Abigail, Nabal's wise wife, intercedes with gifts and persuasion to prevent David from taking revenge, and after Nabal dies ten days later, David marries her.

headings.text: The Death of Samuel David, Nabal, and Abigail

stories.title: ⛰️ 1 Samuel 26
summaryBullets: Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, “Is not David hiding on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon?” (26:1).
So Saul, accompanied by three thousand chosen men of Israel, went down to the Wilderness of Ziph to search for David there. (26:2).
Saul camped beside the road at the hill of Hachilah opposite Jeshimon, but David was living in the wilderness. When he realized that Saul had followed him there, (26:3).
David sent out spies to verify that Saul had arrived. (26:4).

Then David set out and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw the place where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the general of his army, had lain down. Saul was lying inside the inner circle of the camp, with the troops camped around him. (26:5).
And David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?” “I will go with you,” answered Abishai. (26:6).

That night David and Abishai came to the troops, and Saul was lying there asleep in the inner circle of the camp, with his spear stuck in the ground by his head. And Abner and the troops were lying around him. (26:7).

Abishai said to David, “Today God has delivered your enemy into your hand. Now, therefore, please let me thrust the spear through him into the ground with one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice!” (26:8).
But David said to Abishai, “Do not destroy him, for who can extend a hand against the LORD’s anointed and be guiltless?” (26:9).
David added, “As surely as the LORD lives, the LORD Himself will strike him down; either his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and perish. (26:10).
But the LORD forbid that I should extend my hand against the LORD’s anointed. Instead, take the spear and water jug by his head, and let us go.” (26:11).

So David took the spear and water jug by Saul’s head, and they departed. No one saw them or knew about it, nor did anyone wake up; they all remained asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them. (26:12).
Then David crossed to the other side and stood atop the mountain at a distance; there was a wide gulf between them. (26:13).
And David shouted to the troops and to Abner son of Ner, “Will you not answer me, Abner?” “Who are you who calls to the king?” Abner replied. (26:14).
So David said to Abner, “You are a man, aren’t you? And who in Israel is your equal? Why then did you not protect your lord the king when one of the people came to destroy him? (26:15).

This thing you have done is not good. As surely as the LORD lives, all of you deserve to die, since you did not protect your lord, the LORD’s anointed. Now look around. Where are the king’s spear and water jug that were by his head?” (26:16).
Then Saul recognized David’s voice and asked, “Is that your voice, David my son?” “It is my voice, my lord and king,” David said. (26:17).
And he continued, “Why is my lord pursuing his servant? What have I done? What evil is in my hand? (26:18).

Now please, may my lord the king hear the words of his servant: If the LORD has stirred you up against me, then may He accept an offering. But if men have done it, may they be cursed in the presence of the LORD! For today they have driven me away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’ (26:19).
So do not let my blood fall to the ground far from the presence of the LORD. For the king of Israel has come out to look for a flea, like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains.” (26:20).

Then Saul replied, “I have sinned. Come back, David my son. I will never harm you again, because today you considered my life precious. I have played the fool and have committed a grave error!” (26:21).
“Here is the king’s spear,” David answered. “Let one of the young men come over and get it. (26:22).
May the LORD repay every man for his righteousness and faithfulness. For the LORD delivered you into my hand today, but I would not extend my hand against the LORD’s anointed. (26:23).
As surely as I valued your life today, so may the LORD value my life and rescue me from all trouble.” (26:24).
Saul said to him, “May you be blessed, David my son. You will accomplish great things and will surely prevail.” So David went on his way, and Saul returned home. (26:25).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 24:1-7: David cuts the corner of Saul's robe in the cave and is stricken in his heart for it.
Exodus 22:28: You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.
Genesis 2:21: The LORD God causes a deep sleep to fall on the man, the same word used of Saul's camp in verse 12.
Deuteronomy 4:26-28: Driven out from the LORD's inheritance, you will serve gods of wood and stone made by human hands.
2 Samuel 1:14-16: David executes the Amalekite who claimed to have killed the LORD's anointed.

translationNotes.term: The inner circle of the camp
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַעְגָּל (magal), a circle or ring
translationNotes.note: Verses 5 and 7 describe how an army slept in the field. The men lay in a ring with the commander in the middle, sometimes behind a barrier of baggage or carts, so that anyone reaching him had to pass the whole force. That is the point of the chapter: David and Abishai walk in through three thousand sleeping men, stand over the king, and take his spear and his water jug from beside his head. Verse 12 says a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen on them.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה (meshiach YHWH) - Greek (LXX): χριστὸς κυρίου (christos kyriou)
translationNotes.note: Mashiach means smeared or anointed with oil, and it is the title of the man God has installed in office, not a description of his character; David uses it of a king who is at that moment hunting him with three thousand men. His argument in verses 9 to 11 is that the office is God's to give and God's to end, and he says the same thing three ways: the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down in battle. The Greek translation of this exact phrase is christos kyriou, the Lord's Christ.

Verse 6 names Abishai as the son of Zeruiah and the brother of Joab, and Scripture always identifies these three brothers by their mother, never by a father. 1 Chronicles 2:16 explains why it matters: Zeruiah was David's own sister, so Joab, Abishai and Asahel are the king's nephews. That family tie is behind everything they do, including the killings David cannot punish and complains about at 2 Samuel 3:39, the sons of Zeruiah are too harsh for me.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נַחֲלַת יְהוָה (nachalat YHWH), the inheritance of the LORD
translationNotes.note: David's complaint in verse 19 rests on an idea a modern reader has to be told. Gods were thought to belong to territories, so driving a man out of the LORD's land was understood as pushing him into someone else's god's jurisdiction, whether anyone said the words or not. Naaman works from the same assumption when he asks for two mule-loads of Israelite earth to take home to Damascus so he can worship the LORD on it (2 Kings 5:17). Being exiled meant being cut off from where God was worshipped.

stories.keyTakeaway: David sneaks into Saul's sleeping camp with Abishai, refuses to kill the defenseless king despite having the chance, and instead takes Saul's spear and water jug to prove his loyalty; from a distance David confronts Saul, who acknowledges his wrongdoing and promises to stop pursuing him.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 27
summaryBullets: David, however, said to himself, “One of these days now I will be swept away by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than to escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will stop searching for me all over Israel, and I will slip out of his hand.” (27:1).
So David set out with his six hundred men and went to Achish son of Maoch, the king of Gath. (27:2).
David and his men settled in Gath with Achish. Each man had his family with him, and David had his two wives: Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail of Carmel, the widow of Nabal. (27:3).
And when Saul learned that David had fled to Gath, he no longer searched for him. (27:4).

Then David said to Achish, “If I have found favor in your eyes, let me be assigned a place in one of the outlying towns, so I can live there. For why should your servant live in the royal city with you?” (27:5).
That day Achish gave him Ziklag, and to this day it still belongs to the kings of Judah. (27:6).
And the time that David lived in Philistine territory amounted to a year and four months. (27:7).
Now David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites. (From ancient times these people had inhabited the land extending to Shur and Egypt.) (27:8).
Whenever David attacked a territory, he did not leave a man or woman alive, but he took the flocks and herds, the donkeys, camels, and clothing. Then he would return to Achish, (27:9).
who would ask him, “What have you raided today?” And David would reply, “The Negev of Judah,” or “The Negev of Jerahmeel,” or “The Negev of the Kenites.” (27:10).

David did not leave a man or woman alive to be brought to Gath, for he said, “Otherwise they will report us, saying, ‘This is what David did.’” And this was David’s custom the whole time he lived in Philistine territory. (27:11).
So Achish trusted David, thinking, “Since he has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel, he will be my servant forever.” (27:12).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 21:10-15: David's first flight to Achish at Gath, where he escaped by feigning madness.
Joshua 13:2-3: The land still unconquered, including the five Philistine lords and the Geshurites in the south.
Joshua 15:31: Ziklag listed among the towns given to Judah in the Negeb toward the border of Edom.
1 Chronicles 12:1-7,19-22: The fighting men who came over to David at Ziklag while he was kept away from Saul.
Exodus 17:14-16: The LORD swears that He will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.

translationNotes.note: Verses 2 to 3 have David take six hundred men and their households into the service of the king of Gath, the same city he had fled from in disguise six chapters earlier. Hiring a foreign war-band and settling it on your frontier was standard practice: the band gets land and pay, the king gets a buffer and men who have nowhere else to go. Achish believes David has made himself so hated in Israel that he will be his servant for ever (verse 12), and it is this arrangement that puts David in the Philistine order of battle in chapter 29.

Verse 10 lists the districts David claims to be raiding: the Negev of Judah, of the Jerahmeelites, of the Kenites. The dry south was divided into named clan districts, and both those clans were reckoned with Judah, the Jerahmeelites descended from Judah's own line (1 Chronicles 2:9, 25) and the Kenites long settled among them (Judges 1:16). So the answer he gives Achish means he has been attacking his own people, which is a lie, and a well-chosen one.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְבִלְתִּי הַגִּיד (le-bilti haggid), so as not to report
translationNotes.note: Verses 9 and 11 state the reason without dressing it up: David killed every man and woman in the places he raided so that nobody could reach Gath and say what he had actually been doing. The text calls it his practice for the whole time he lived in Philistine country, sixteen months. It is reported flatly, as a piece of what it cost to survive on that border, and the writer neither excuses it nor comments on it.

A town in the dry Negev country south of Gath, handed to David by Achish and held by him for a year and four months (verse 7). A Philistine king gave a vassal a border town to make him a buffer against desert raiders, and it also put David outside Saul's reach. Verse 6 notes it stayed the personal property of the kings of Judah from then on.

stories.keyTakeaway: David flees to the Philistine king Achish in Gath, settles in Ziklag, and spends sixteen months raiding neighboring peoples while telling Achish he's attacking Judah; Achish grows confident David will serve him forever.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 28
summaryBullets: Now in those days the Philistines gathered their forces for warfare against Israel. So Achish said to David, “You must understand that you and your men are to go out to battle with me.” (28:1).
David replied, “Then you will come to know what your servant can do.” “Very well,” said Achish. “I will make you my bodyguard for life.” (28:2).
Now by this time Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land. (28:3).
The Philistines gathered together and camped at Shunem, while Saul gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa. (28:4).
When Saul saw the Philistine army, he was afraid and trembled violently. (28:5).
He inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him by dreams or Urim or prophets. (28:6).
Then Saul said to his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her.” “There is a medium at Endor,” his servants replied. (28:7).

So Saul disguised himself by putting on different clothes, and he set out with two of his men. They came to the woman at night, and Saul said, “Consult a spirit for me. Bring up for me the one I name.” (28:8).
But the woman replied, “Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has killed the mediums and spiritists in the land. Why have you set a trap to get me killed?” (28:9).
Then Saul swore to her by the LORD: “As surely as the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this.” (28:10).
“Whom shall I bring up for you?” the woman asked. “Bring up Samuel,” he replied. (28:11).
But when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out in a loud voice and said to Saul, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!” (28:12).
“Do not be afraid,” the king replied. “What do you see?” “I see a god coming up out of the earth,” the woman answered. (28:13).
“What does he look like?” asked Saul. “An old man is coming up,” she replied. “And he is wearing a robe.” So Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed facedown in reverence. (28:14).

Then Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?” “I am deeply distressed,” replied Saul. “The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either by prophets or by dreams. So I have called on you to tell me what to do.” (28:15).
“Why do you consult me,” asked Samuel, “since the LORD has turned away from you and become your enemy? (28:16).
He has done exactly what He spoke through me: The LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor David. (28:17).
Because you did not obey the LORD or carry out His burning anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today. (28:18).

Moreover, the LORD will deliver Israel with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. And the LORD will deliver the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.” (28:19).
Immediately Saul fell flat on the ground, terrified by the words of Samuel. And his strength was gone, because he had not eaten anything all that day and night. (28:20).
When the woman came to Saul and saw how distraught he was, she said to him, “Look, your maidservant has obeyed your voice. I took my life in my hands and did as you told me. (28:21).
Now please listen to your servant and let me set a morsel of bread before you so you may eat and have the strength to go on your way.” (28:22).
Saul refused, saying, “I will not eat.” But his servants joined the woman in urging him, and he heeded their voice. He got up from the ground and sat on the bed. (28:23).
The woman had a fattened calf at her house, and she quickly slaughtered it. She also took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread. (28:24).
She served it to Saul and his servants, and they ate. And that night they got up and left. (28:25).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 18:9-14: Do not practise divination, omens, sorcery, or consult a medium or the dead; all who do so are detestable to the LORD.
Leviticus 19:31: Do not turn to mediums or necromancers, and do not seek them out, to be defiled by them.
Leviticus 20:6,27: The person who turns to mediums will be cut off, and a medium or necromancer is to be put to death.
1 Samuel 15:22-29: Samuel tells Saul the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from him and given it to a neighbour better than he.
1 Chronicles 10:13-14: Saul died for his unfaithfulness and for consulting a medium, and the LORD turned the kingdom to David.

translationNotes.note: An ov is one who consults the dead on someone's behalf, and the practice is banned outright with the penalty attached: Leviticus 19:31 forbids turning to them, 20:6 sets God's face against anyone who does, and 20:27 makes it a capital offence for the practitioner. Deuteronomy 18:9-14 lists it with divination, sorcery and child sacrifice as the reason the nations were driven out, and promises a prophet instead. Verse 3 notes that Saul had cleared them out of the land himself, which is why the woman at Endor has to be found and why he goes at night in disguise.

translationNotes.term: No answer by dreams, Urim or prophets
translationNotes.note: Verse 6 names the three channels God had given, and says all three are shut. Dreams could come to anyone (Genesis 41:25, Numbers 12:6); the Urim was the yes-or-no enquiry made through the high priest's breastpiece; the prophets spoke direct. Saul had destroyed the priesthood at Nob himself and the ephod is with David (22:20, 23:6), Samuel is dead, and the chapter puts the silence and the seance side by side without comment.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים (elohim), a divine being - מְעִיל (meil), robe
translationNotes.note: Verse 13 has the woman say she sees elohim coming up out of the earth, a word for a divine or supernatural being, and verse 14 has Saul identify Samuel from the description of an old man wrapped in a robe. The robe is the detail that settles it for Saul, because a meil is the garment Samuel had worn since he was a boy at Shiloh and the one Saul had torn in 15:27. From verse 15 onward the text simply calls him Samuel and reports his words as a message from the LORD, and everything he says comes to pass the next day.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: עֵגֶל־מַרְבֵּק (egel marbeq), a stall-fed calf
translationNotes.note: Verses 24 and 25 close the chapter with a meal, and the animal named is the most expensive thing a household could put on a table. A stall-fed calf was penned and grain-fed rather than left to graze, kept for an occasion; Abraham kills one for his three visitors (Genesis 18:7), and it is the animal the father calls for in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:23). The woman Saul had outlawed feeds him, with bread baked while he waits, and gets him back on his feet to walk to the battle in which he dies.

A village on the far side of the hill of Moreh, across the Jezreel valley from Mount Gilboa. The Philistine army lay between Saul's camp and Endor, which is why verse 8 has him travel by night in disguise; he had to go around an enemy line to reach a woman he had himself outlawed. The trip is about seven or eight miles of open valley.

stories.keyTakeaway: Saul, terrified before battle with the Philistines and abandoned by God, disguises himself and visits a medium in Endor to summon Samuel, who tells him the kingdom has been given to David and that Saul and his sons will die in tomorrow's battle. After hearing this prophecy, Saul collapses in despair; the medium feeds him and his men before they depart.

headings.text: Saul and the Medium of Endor

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 29
summaryBullets: Now the Philistines brought all their forces together at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel. (29:1).
As the Philistine leaders marched out with their units of hundreds and thousands, David and his men marched behind them with Achish. (29:2).

Then the commanders of the Philistines asked, “What about these Hebrews?” Achish replied, “Is this not David, the servant of King Saul of Israel? He has been with me all these days, even years, and from the day he defected until today I have found no fault in him.” (29:3).

But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with Achish and told him, “Send that man back and let him return to the place you assigned him. He must not go down with us into battle only to become our adversary during the war. What better way for him to regain the favor of his master than with the heads of our men? (29:4).
Is this not the David about whom they sing in their dances: ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?” (29:5).

So Achish summoned David and told him, “As surely as the LORD lives, you have been upright, and it seems right in my sight that you should march in and out with me in the army, because I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until this day. But you are not good in the sight of the leaders. (29:6).
Therefore turn back now and go in peace, so that you will not do anything to displease the leaders of the Philistines.” (29:7).

“But what have I done?” David replied. “What have you found against your servant, from the day I came to you until today, to keep me from going along to fight against the enemies of my lord the king?” (29:8).
Achish replied, “I know that you are as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God. But the commanders of the Philistines have said, ‘He must not go into battle with us.’ (29:9).
Now then, get up early in the morning, along with your master’s servants who came with you, and go as soon as it is light.” (29:10).
So David and his men got up early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. And the Philistines went up to Jezreel. (29:11).
crossRefs: 1 Samuel 18:6-9: The women sing that Saul struck down thousands and David tens of thousands, the song the Philistine lords quote here.
1 Samuel 21:10-15: David's earlier appearance at Gath, when Achish's own servants called him the king of the land.
1 Samuel 4:1: Israel camps at Ebenezer and the Philistines at Aphek, the same mustering ground as verse 1 here.
1 Samuel 27:8-12: David's raids in the far south and the false reports he had been giving Achish about them.
Joshua 12:18: The king of Aphek listed among the kings west of the Jordan whom Joshua defeated.

translationNotes.note: Verse 2 is a formal review. The five Philistine rulers bring their contingents past in units of hundreds and thousands, each lord leading his own men, which is how an army made up of five allied cities assembled and how its commanders saw what everyone had brought. Israel used the same divisions, thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (Exodus 18:21, 1 Samuel 8:12). David and his six hundred come past at the rear, with Achish, in full view of every other commander.

The word the Philistine commanders use in verse 4 is satan, and here it is an ordinary noun meaning an opponent or someone who obstructs you; the same word is used of the human enemies God raises up against Solomon (1 Kings 11:14, 23) and of a man standing to accuse in court (Psalm 109:6). Their fear is concrete: a contingent that changes sides in the middle of a battle. English readers who meet the word only as a name will miss what is being said about David.

Verse 5 has Philistine officers quote the Israelite victory couplet back word for word, Saul has slain his thousands and David his tens of thousands. It had already been quoted to Achish by his own servants when David came to Gath as a fugitive (21:11). A song sung by women in the towns of Israel is being used, years later, as intelligence at an enemy council of war, and it is what gets David sent home.

translationNotes.term: As blameless as an angel of God
translationNotes.note: Achish's words in verse 9 are court language, not theology. Comparing a man to a messenger of God was a set compliment paid to someone whose judgment or loyalty was beyond question, and it is used three times to David himself once he is king (2 Samuel 14:17, 14:20, 19:27). The irony is that Achish means it, and the reader has just read chapter 27.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Philistine commanders refuse to let David fight alongside them against Israel, fearing he will turn against them in battle; Achish sends David and his men back, and they depart early in the morning.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 30
summaryBullets: On the third day David and his men arrived in Ziklag, and the Amalekites had raided the Negev, attacked Ziklag, and burned it down. (30:1).
They had taken captive the women and all who were there, both young and old. They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way. (30:2).
When David and his men came to the city, they found it burned down and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive. (30:3).
So David and the troops with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep. (30:4).
David’s two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel, had been taken captive. (30:5).
And David was greatly distressed because the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of every man grieved for his sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God. (30:6).
Then David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, “Bring me the ephod.” So Abiathar brought it to him, (30:7).
and David inquired of the LORD: “Should I pursue these raiders? Will I overtake them?” “Pursue them,” the LORD replied, “for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives.” (30:8).
So David and his six hundred men went to the Brook of Besor, where some stayed behind (30:9).
because two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook. But David and four hundred men continued in pursuit. (30:10).
Now his men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave the man water to drink and food to eat — (30:11).
a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins. So he ate and was revived, for he had not had any food or water for three days and three nights. (30:12).
Then David asked him, “To whom do you belong, and where are you from?” “I am an Egyptian,” he replied, “the slave of an Amalekite. My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill. (30:13).
We raided the Negev of the Cherethites, the territory of Judah, and the Negev of Caleb, and we burned down Ziklag.” (30:14).
“Will you lead me to these raiders?” David asked. And the man replied, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master, and I will lead you to them.” (30:15).

So he led David down, and there were the Amalekites spread out over all the land, eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah. (30:16).
And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day. Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels. (30:17).
So David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives. (30:18).
Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken. David brought everything back. (30:19).
And he took all the flocks and herds, which his men drove ahead of the other livestock, calling out, “This is David’s plunder!” (30:20).

When David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow him and who were left behind at the Brook of Besor, they came out to meet him and the troops with him. As David approached the men, he greeted them, (30:21).

but all the wicked and worthless men among those who had gone with David said, “Because they did not go with us, we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man’s wife and children. They may take them and go.” (30:22).
But David said, “My brothers, you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us. (30:23).
Who will listen to your proposal? The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike.” (30:24).
And so it has been from that day forward. David established this statute and ordinance for Israel to this very day. (30:25).
When David arrived in Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies.” (30:26).
He sent gifts to those in Bethel, Ramoth Negev, and Jattir; (30:27).
to those in Aroer, Siphmoth, and Eshtemoa; (30:28).
to those in Racal and in the cities of the Jerahmeelites and Kenites; (30:29).
to those in Hormah, Bor-ashan, and Athach; (30:30).
and to those in Hebron and in all the places where David and his men had roamed. (30:31).
crossRefs: Numbers 31:25-27: The plunder is divided evenly between the men who went out to the battle and the rest of the congregation.
Joshua 22:8: Return to your tents with much livestock and spoil, and divide it with your brothers.
Exodus 17:8-16: Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim, and the LORD swears war with Amalek from generation to generation.
1 Samuel 15:1-9: Saul is sent to destroy Amalek and spares Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle.
Deuteronomy 23:15-16: A slave who has escaped to you shall not be handed back to his master, but may live wherever he chooses.

translationNotes.note: Verses 9 and 10 stop the pursuit at a wadi running west to the sea through the dry country south of Gaza. A wadi in that country is a steep-sided channel, dry most of the year, and getting six hundred men with weapons down one side and up the other is hard work at the end of a forced march; two hundred of them cannot do it. The place is named because of what it decides, and the argument in verses 21 to 25 is about those two hundred men.

translationNotes.term: A share for the man who stays with the baggage
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֹק וּמִשְׁפָּט (choq u-mishpat), a statute and an ordinance
translationNotes.note: Verses 23 to 25 settle a question armies had always fought over, and David settles it as law. The share of the man who goes down to the battle and the share of the man who stays with the supplies are equal, because guarding the baggage is part of the operation. Numbers 31:27 had already divided plunder between the men who fought and the rest of the congregation. Verse 25 says it became a fixed statute in Israel from that day on.

translationNotes.term: Presents to the elders of Judah
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בְּרָכָה (berakhah), a blessing or gift
translationNotes.note: Verses 26 to 31 look like a list to skip and are the political heart of the chapter. David sends a share of the plunder to the elders of a dozen and more towns across the south of Judah, calling it a gift from the plunder of the LORD's enemies. Distributing spoil to town elders is how a leader built obligation in a society without offices or taxes, and these are the towns whose men come to Hebron and make him king of Judah in 2 Samuel 2:4.

translationNotes.term: Left for dead in a field
translationNotes.note: The Amalekites abandon a sick Egyptian slave three days from water (verses 11 to 13), and David's men give him bread, a cake of figs, two clusters of raisins, and water. Pressed fig and raisin cakes were the standard travel ration because they keep, carry, and restore a starving man fast. The slave's directions are what find the raiders.

stories.keyTakeaway: David returns to find Ziklag burned and his wives taken by Amalekites; after consulting God through the ephod, he pursues them with four hundred men, recovers all the captives and plunder, and establishes a law that those who guard supplies share equally in the spoils. He then distributes portions of the recovered goods to the elders of Judah.

stories.title: ⚔️ 1 Samuel 31
summaryBullets: Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before them, and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa. (31:1).
The Philistines hotly pursued Saul and his sons, and they killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. (31:2).
When the battle intensified against Saul, the archers overtook him and wounded him critically. (31:3).

Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through with it, or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and torture me!” But his armor-bearer was terrified and refused to do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it. (31:4).
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died with him. (31:5).
So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day. (31:6).

When the Israelites along the valley and those on the other side of the Jordan saw that the army of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and ran away. So the Philistines came and occupied their cities. (31:7).
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. (31:8).
They cut off Saul’s head, stripped off his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temples of their idols and among their people. (31:9).
They put his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan. (31:10).
When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, (31:11).
all their men of valor set out, journeyed all night, and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan. When they arrived at Jabesh, they burned the bodies there. (31:12).
Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days. (31:13).
crossRefs: 1 Chronicles 10:1-14: The parallel account, closing with the reason for Saul's death: his unfaithfulness and his consulting a medium.
1 Samuel 28:19: Samuel tells Saul that tomorrow he and his sons will be with him and Israel will be given into Philistine hands.
1 Samuel 11:1-11: Saul marches all night to break the siege of Jabesh-gilead, the debt those men repay here.
2 Samuel 1:17-27: David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, how the mighty have fallen, tell it not in Gath.
Judges 1:27: Manasseh did not drive out the people of Beth-shan and its villages, and the Canaanites remained in that land.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וְהִתְעַלְּלוּ־בִי (ve-hitallelu vi), and they will make sport of me
translationNotes.note: Saul's reason in verse 4 is the fate of a captured king, and it was not imagined. The Philistines blinded Samson, chained him and brought him out to entertain a full house (Judges 16:21-25); Nebuchadnezzar killed Zedekiah's sons in front of him and then put out his eyes (2 Kings 25:7). Verses 9 and 10 show what they did with the body they got: head cut off, armour sent round the temples as an announcement, and the corpse fastened to a city wall.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיִּפֹּל עָלֶיהָ (vayyippol aleha), and he fell on it
translationNotes.note: Verse 4 records four things in order: Saul asks his armour-bearer to run him through, the man refuses out of fear, Saul falls on his own sword, and the armour-bearer does the same when he sees the king dead. Scripture reports very few suicides and never pauses to comment on them; the others are Ahithophel (2 Samuel 17:23), Zimri (1 Kings 16:18) and Judas (Matthew 27:5). An armour-bearer's job was to carry the shield and spare weapons and to finish the wounded, which is why the request is made to him.

Israel buried its dead; burning a body was a penalty reserved for particular crimes (Leviticus 20:14, 21:9) and Amos 2:1 counts burning a king's bones as an atrocity when Moab does it. So verse 12 is unusual, and verse 13 shows what it was for: the men of Jabesh-gilead burned what the Philistines had left after days on the wall, then buried the bones under the tamarisk at Jabesh and fasted seven days. David later moved the bones to the family grave at Zela (2 Samuel 21:12-14).

A ridge rising to about 1,700 feet on the southeast rim of the Jezreel Valley. The valley below is the one wide, flat corridor across northern Israel, which is chariot country and the ground Israel could least afford to fight on. Saul had to meet the Philistines there because the valley cuts his kingdom in two, and the archers on the slope broke his line (verse 3).

A fortified mound where the Jezreel Valley meets the Jordan Valley, controlling the crossing east and the road north, about fifteen miles from Gilboa. Egypt garrisoned it for centuries and Israel never took it (Judges 1:27), so it was in Philistine hands. Verse 10 has Saul's body and his sons' fastened to its wall and his armour placed in the temple of Ashtoreth, a public display on the busiest road in the north.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Philistines defeat Israel in battle; Saul and his three sons are killed, and their bodies are mutilated and displayed, though the men of Jabesh Gilead later retrieve and bury them.

intro:
1 Samuel was written by the prophets Samuel, Nathan, and Gad, according to 1 Chronicles 29:29, which records that "the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the records of Samuel the seer, the records of Nathan the prophet, and the records of Gad the seer." Samuel composed the earlier portions covering his own life and ministry; Nathan and Gad, court prophets during David's reign, contributed the later material. The book reached its final form around 1000-960 BC, during or shortly after David's reign in Jerusalem. Samuel was born in the hill country of Ephraim to Hannah, raised at the Tabernacle in Shiloh under Eli the high priest, and served as judge, prophet, and kingmaker over Israel. Nathan was the court prophet under David, the one who confronted David over Bathsheba and Uriah, who delivered the Davidic covenant promise (2 Samuel 7), and who later helped install Solomon as king (1 Kings 1). Gad was David's personal seer (2 Samuel 24:11) who advised him from the early cave-fugitive years through the end of his reign. The events of the book span roughly 1100 to 1011 BC, from Samuel's birth through Saul's death on Mount Gilboa. The historical setting is Iron Age I in Canaan, with Israel's tribal confederacy transitioning into a centralized monarchy under threat from the Philistine pentapolis (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath) along the coastal plain, the Amalekites in the Negev, and the Ammonites east of the Jordan. Egypt's New Kingdom had collapsed and the Late Bronze Age powers had given way to smaller regional kingdoms of the early Iron Age.

1 Samuel and 2 Samuel were originally a single Hebrew book called Shmuel ("Samuel"), named for the prophet who composed its earliest portions and the first major figure of the narrative. The Greek Septuagint translators (3rd century BC) divided the book into two and grouped it with Kings as "1-4 Kingdoms" (or "Reigns"); the Latin Vulgate followed this division with the names "1-2 Samuel" and "1-2 Kings," and English Bibles inherited that arrangement. In the Jewish canon, Samuel is the third book of the Former Prophets (Nevi'im Rishonim). Hebrew manuscript fragments of Samuel were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), with copies dating to the 3rd century BC and later.
